title: Could eating jellyfish be sustainable
paragraphs: While giant sharks are more common sea monsters in films, jellyfish also pose a major threat in real life – with some able to kill people with their stings. And the potential danger they cause doesn’t stop there, with reports of them attacking salmon farms, shutting down power stations and incapacitating warships. There are even some scientists in Australia researching whether box jellyfish could ultimately destroy our oceans – so could devouring them be a possible solution?

The huge number of jellyfish in our oceans means that if we did start eating them, there is already a large supply of these potential morsels to be dined on. Also, some people argue that due to their reproductive cycle, jellyfish are actually a sustainable food source. Removing a jellyfish from the ocean doesn’t stop new ones being born. This is because they are spawned from polyps on the seabed. In some ways, you can compare them to apples. When you take an apple from a tree, the tree still goes on to produce more apples.

What about their nutritional value? Jellyfish contain 36 calories per ounce, which puts it on a par with iceberg lettuce. However, unlike lettuce, it is full of protein, making it potentially a great diet food. And indeed, in many parts of the world, particularly in Asia, they are already consumed, often raw, fried or chopped up as part of a salad. The demand for these animals, combined with their numbers, means that selling jellyfish is becoming an ever more lucrative business.

But what do they taste like? While some say they are flavourless, others describe them as having a salty taste. This could be due to their absorbent nature, which also leads them to being often served in a sauce. As for the texture, some people negatively compare the experience to eating gristle.

So, the next time you fancy chowing down on some fish, you might look at jellyfish as a sustainable alternative. They might not be the tastiest thing you’ve ever eaten, but it beats fleeing the sea to avoid being stung.

title: What makes us late
paragraphs: As the saying goes, ‘time waits for no man’. Time is always against us, and we just can’t stop it. Maybe that’s why some of us are always running late for appointments. But if timekeeping is not what you’re good at, don’t stress. There might be a good reason for your lack of punctuality.

People’s attitudes to being on time vary. Some clock-watch and make sure they’re bang on time for a meeting. It is, after all, rude to be late, and if you can make it on time, why can’t everyone else? But if, like me, you want to make every second count, you might try to squeeze as much as you can into the time you have available. However, when your schedule doesn’t run to plan, your punctuality inevitably slips.

People who lack promptness have been described as ‘time benders’. Author Grace Pacie told the BBC that “they’re the people who don’t want to be late, but they have a strange resistance to being early, and they don’t allow enough time.” They assume their journey to an appointment will always go smoothly, and the train will always be on time!

Perceptions of unpunctual people are almost always negative – even if sometimes wrong. Writing for the BBC, Laura Clarke says: “Being consistently late might not be your fault. It could be your type. The punctually-challenged often share personality characteristics, such as optimism, low levels of self-control, anxiety, or a penchant for thrill-seeking, experts say. It is also possible people are late so not to be conspicuous and to avoid the anxious wait for others to turn up.

Maybe us latecomers should make more of an effort and follow the advice I heard to not ‘try’ to be on time but ‘decide’ to be on time. But I know if a meeting or a deadline really matters, then I’ll be there. Otherwise relax, even if others are cursing you!

title: What makes us afraid
paragraphs: What are the things that scare you: snakes, spiders or creepy crawlies? Or maybe you have a fear of heights or visiting the dentist. Although some of us just get scared or a bit nervous about these things, for others it can cause an irrational reaction that can’t be controlled – something we call a phobia. It occurs when someone develops an exaggerated or unrealistic sense of danger about a situation or object.

Sometimes it’s good to be aware of the possible dangers from things. Our brain alerts us to the risks that might lie ahead, but then we often rationalise the risks and overcome them. Clinical psychologist Warren Mansell told the BBC: “Our fears are hard-wired into our brains – we don’t need to learn to be afraid of animals like snakes or spiders.” But phobias are stronger than just fears. Warren says: “An area called the amygdala in the brain is recognising a threat and preparing your body for fight or flight.” With a phobia, your breathing gets quicker, your pulse speeds up, you sweat, there’s more glucose in your blood, increasing your energy, and your brain is unable to control these reactions.

But where does a phobia come from? Speaking to the BBC, Lauren Rosenberg, a fear and phobia expert, says: “Phobias usually are a copy behaviour from a higher authority, like a parent or teacher, or something you have learnt from your own experience.” Or a trauma from a past event that comes back to haunt you.

There are many different complex phobias some people suffer from, such as agoraphobia – triggered by being away from home, social anxiety disorder – feeling anxious in social situations, and iatrophobia – fear of doctors. But how can they be overcome? Cognitive behavioural therapy is one option, where you gradually get used to whatever it is you fear. Lauren Rosenburg says she likes to work with people to clear their subconscious memory and help them breathe. But if you do have a phobia, continually trying to avoid what you’re afraid of is likely to make the situation worse, so it’s a good idea to find help to overcome it.

title: The future of electric cars
paragraphs: We are all aware of the damaging pollution that’s created by driving petrol and diesel vehicles. Many of the world’s cities are clogged with traffic, creating fumes containing gases such as nitrogen oxides. The solution for a cleaner, greener future could be electric vehicles. But how optimistic should we be?

There was much excitement last year when the UK government announced it will ban the sale of new petrol and diesel cars from 2030. But is that easier said than done? The road to global traffic being totally electric is still a long way off. Currently, battery life is an issue – a fully charged battery won’t take you as far as a full tank of petrol. There are also limited numbers of charging points to plug an EV into.

Of course, technology is always improving. Some of the biggest tech companies, like Google and Tesla, are spending huge amounts of money developing electric cars. And most of the big car manufacturers are now making them too. Colin Herron, a consultant on low-carbon vehicle technology, told the BBC: “The big leap forward will come with solid state batteries, which will appear first in mobile phones and laptops before they progress to cars.” These will charge more quickly and give cars a bigger range.

Cost is another issue that may deter people switching to electric power. But some countries offer incentives, such as cutting prices by reducing import taxes, and not charging for road tax and parking. Some also provide exclusive lanes for electric cars to be driven on, overtaking traditional cars which might be stuck in jams. These kinds of measures have made Norway the country with the most electric cars per capita at more than thirty electric cars per 1000 inhabitants.

But Colin Herron warns that ‘electric motoring’ doesn’t mean a zero-carbon future. “It’s emission-free motoring, but the car has to be built, the battery has to be built, and the electricity does come from somewhere.” Maybe it’s time to think about making fewer journeys or using public transport.

sentences.english: We are all aware of the damaging pollution that’s created by driving petrol and diesel vehicles.
sentences.chinese: 我们都清楚，驾驶汽油车和柴油车会产生有害污染。

sentences.english: Many of the world’s cities are clogged with traffic, creating fumes containing gases such as nitrogen oxides.
sentences.chinese: 世界上许多城市都被交通拥堵所困扰，车辆排放的尾气中含有氮氧化物等气体。

sentences.english: The solution for a cleaner, greener future could be electric vehicles.
sentences.chinese: 想要实现更清洁、更环保的未来，电动汽车或许是一个解决方案。

sentences.english: But how optimistic should we be?
sentences.chinese: 但我们对此应该持多乐观的态度呢？

sentences.english: There was much excitement last year when the UK government announced it will ban the sale of new petrol and diesel cars from 2030.
sentences.chinese: 去年英国政府宣布将从2030年起禁止销售新的汽油车和柴油车时，人们都感到十分振奋。

sentences.english: But is that easier said than done?
sentences.chinese: 但这件事真的是说起来容易做起来难吗？

sentences.english: The road to global traffic being totally electric is still a long way off.
sentences.chinese: 要实现全球交通全面电动化，还有很长的路要走。

sentences.english: Currently, battery life is an issue – a fully charged battery won’t take you as far as a full tank of petrol.
sentences.chinese: 目前，电池续航能力是一大问题——一块充满电的电池，续航里程远不及一箱汽油。

sentences.english: There are also limited numbers of charging points to plug an EV into.
sentences.chinese: 此外，可供电动汽车充电的充电桩数量也十分有限。

sentences.english: Of course, technology is always improving.
sentences.chinese: 当然，技术一直在不断进步。

sentences.english: Some of the biggest tech companies, like Google and Tesla, are spending huge amounts of money developing electric cars. And most of the big car manufacturers are now making them too.
sentences.chinese: 谷歌、特斯拉等大型科技公司都在投入巨资研发电动汽车，大多数主流汽车制造商如今也开始生产电动汽车。

sentences.english: Colin Herron, a consultant on low-carbon vehicle technology, told the BBC: “The big leap forward will come with solid state batteries, which will appear first in mobile phones and laptops before they progress to cars.”
sentences.chinese: 低碳汽车技术顾问科林·赫伦在接受BBC采访时表示：“固态电池的出现将会带来巨大的技术飞跃，这类电池会率先应用于手机和笔记本电脑，之后才会推广到汽车领域。”

sentences.english: These will charge more quickly and give cars a bigger range.
sentences.chinese: 固态电池充电速度更快，还能为汽车带来更长的续航里程。

sentences.english: Cost is another issue that may deter people switching to electric power.
sentences.chinese: 成本是另一个可能阻碍人们转向电动汽车的因素。

sentences.english: But some countries offer incentives, such as cutting prices by reducing import taxes, and not charging for road tax and parking.
sentences.chinese: 但一些国家推出了激励政策，比如通过降低进口税来压低车价，免除车辆的道路税和停车费。

sentences.english: Some also provide exclusive lanes for electric cars to be driven on, overtaking traditional cars which might be stuck in jams.
sentences.chinese: 部分国家还专门设置了电动汽车专用车道，让电动汽车可以超越那些可能陷入拥堵的传统燃油车。

sentences.english: These kinds of measures have made Norway the country with the most electric cars per capita at more than thirty electric cars per 1000 inhabitants.
sentences.chinese: 这类政策让挪威成为了人均电动汽车拥有量最高的国家，每1000名居民所拥有的电动汽车数量超过30辆。

sentences.english: But Colin Herron warns that ‘electric motoring’ doesn’t mean a zero-carbon future.
sentences.chinese: 但科林·赫伦提醒道，“电动汽车出行”并不意味着零碳未来。

sentences.english: “It’s emission-free motoring, but the car has to be built, the battery has to be built, and the electricity does come from somewhere.”
sentences.chinese: “电动汽车行驶时确实不会产生尾气排放，但汽车本身需要制造，电池也需要生产，而且电力也并非凭空而来。”

sentences.english: Maybe it’s time to think about making fewer journeys or using public transport.
sentences.chinese: 或许我们是时候考虑减少出行次数，或是多使用公共交通工具了。

title: Making your gadgets last longer
titleChinese: 延长电子产品的使用寿命
paragraphs: Have you got any gadgets hanging around your home that you no longer want or use? Between us, we have millions of bits of tech stockpiled in drawers that could be given a new lease of life.

Part of the problem for our unloved gadgets is that many become obsolete quickly because their software doesn’t get updated. Other items are left unused because they’re broken or they’ve become superseded by a fancy new version. Many of these items are electronics, but despite them appearing to be past their sell-by date, they don’t need to end up in landfill.

There are several ways to make the most of our unwanted gadgets. Recycling is the obvious solution. Materials used to make them can be extracted and reused in other things. As an example, Elisabeth Ratcliffe from the Royal Society of Chemistry told the BBC: “There are about thirty different elements just in a smartphone, and many of them are very rare.” These can be used in touch screens and solar panels.

Probably the best antidote to our throwaway culture is to repair our broken tech. This takes patience and skill, which can be learnt at repair clubs and repair cafés – free meeting places where you’ll find tools and materials to help you make any repairs you need. In the UK, the interest in mending our stuff and giving it a new life is reflected by the popularity of a TV series called The Repair Shop, where craftspeople rescue and resurrect items their owners thought were beyond saving.

A final option for your discarded gadgets is to upcycle them. You can breathe new life into unwanted stuff by transforming it into valuable pieces or collectable retro items. These could be sold on, meaning you can make some cash from your junk and create much needed space in your home!

vocabulary.entry: gadget /ˈɡædʒɪt/ n. 小型电子产品；小器具
vocabulary.example: This kitchen gadget is very useful for peeling vegetables.
vocabulary.translation: 这款厨房小器具削皮很方便。

vocabulary.entry: stockpile /ˈstɒkpaɪl/ v. 囤积；贮存
vocabulary.example: People tend to stockpile food before bad weather.
vocabulary.translation: 人们会在恶劣天气来临前囤积食物。

vocabulary.entry: new lease of life /njuː liːs ɒv laɪf/ 新生；重焕生机
vocabulary.example: The old building has been given a new lease of life after renovation.
vocabulary.translation: 这座老建筑翻新后重焕生机。

vocabulary.entry: obsolete /ˌɒbsəˈliːt/ adj. 过时的；淘汰的
vocabulary.example: This type of computer is now obsolete.
vocabulary.translation: 这种型号的电脑现在已经过时了。

vocabulary.entry: supersede /ˌsuːpəˈsiːd/ v. 取代；替代
vocabulary.example: Digital cameras have superseded film cameras in most cases.
vocabulary.translation: 数码相机在大多数情况下已经取代了胶片相机。

vocabulary.entry: fancy /ˈfænsi/ adj. 精致的；花哨的
vocabulary.example: She bought a fancy dress for the party.
vocabulary.translation: 她为派对买了一条精致的裙子。

vocabulary.entry: past one's sell-by date /pɑːst wʌnz sel baɪ deɪt/ 过了有效期；失去使用价值
vocabulary.example: This milk is past its sell-by date, so don't drink it.
vocabulary.translation: 这牛奶已经过期了，别喝了。

vocabulary.entry: landfill /ˈlændfɪl/ n. 垃圾填埋场
vocabulary.example: Too much waste is sent to landfill every year.
vocabulary.translation: 每年有太多垃圾被运往填埋场。

vocabulary.entry: make the most of /meɪk ðə məʊst ɒv/ 充分利用
vocabulary.example: We should make the most of the opportunity to learn English.
vocabulary.translation: 我们应该充分利用这个学习英语的机会。

vocabulary.entry: extract /ɪkˈstrækt/ v. 提取；提炼
vocabulary.example: They extract oil from the seeds of this plant.
vocabulary.translation: 他们从这种植物的种子中提取油。

vocabulary.entry: element /ˈelɪmənt/ n. 元素
vocabulary.example: Gold is a precious element that doesn't corrode easily.
vocabulary.translation: 黄金是一种不易腐蚀的贵金属元素。

vocabulary.entry: rare /reə/ adj. 稀有的；罕见的
vocabulary.example: This rare bird is only found in the tropical rainforest.
vocabulary.translation: 这种珍稀鸟类只在热带雨林中出现。

vocabulary.entry: touch screen /tʌtʃ skriːn/ n. 触摸屏
vocabulary.example: The touch screen of this tablet is very responsive.
vocabulary.translation: 这款平板电脑的触摸屏反应很灵敏。

vocabulary.entry: solar panel /ˈsəʊlə ˈpænl/ n. 太阳能电池板
vocabulary.example: The house is equipped with solar panels to generate electricity.
vocabulary.translation: 这座房子装有太阳能电池板发电。

vocabulary.entry: antidote /ˈæntidəʊt/ n. 对策；解毒剂
vocabulary.example: Regular exercise is an effective antidote to stress.
vocabulary.translation: 规律运动是缓解压力的有效对策。

vocabulary.entry: throwaway culture /ˈθrəʊəweɪ ˈkʌltʃə/ 用完即扔的文化
vocabulary.example: We need to reduce waste by changing our throwaway culture.
vocabulary.translation: 我们需要改变用完即扔的文化来减少浪费。

vocabulary.entry: repair café /rɪˈpeə ˈkæfeɪ/ n. 修理咖啡馆
vocabulary.example: The local repair café helps people fix their broken appliances for free.
vocabulary.translation: 这家本地的修理咖啡馆免费帮人们修理损坏的家电。

vocabulary.entry: craftsperson /ˈkrɑːftspɜːsn/ n. 手工艺人
vocabulary.example: The craftsperson carved a beautiful pattern on the wooden box.
vocabulary.translation: 这位手工艺人在木盒上雕刻了精美的图案。

vocabulary.entry: rescue /ˈreskjuː/ v. 拯救；挽救
vocabulary.example: The firefighters managed to rescue three people from the burning building.
vocabulary.translation: 消防员成功从着火的大楼里救出了三个人。

vocabulary.entry: resurrect /ˌrezəˈrekt/ v. 修复；使重获新生
vocabulary.example: The old car was resurrected by the experienced mechanic.
vocabulary.translation: 这辆旧车被经验丰富的机械师修复好了。

vocabulary.entry: beyond saving /bɪˈjɒnd ˈseɪvɪŋ/ 无法挽救；无可救药
vocabulary.example: The damaged painting was thought to be beyond saving.
vocabulary.translation: 这幅受损的画作曾被认为无法挽救。

vocabulary.entry: discarded /dɪˈskɑːdɪd/ adj. 被丢弃的；废弃的
vocabulary.example: She found some discarded furniture on the street.
vocabulary.translation: 她在街上发现了一些被丢弃的家具。

vocabulary.entry: upcycle /ˈʌpsaɪkl/ v. 升级改造（废旧物品）
vocabulary.example: She likes to upcycle old jars into storage containers.
vocabulary.translation: 她喜欢把旧罐子升级改造成收纳盒。

vocabulary.entry: collectable /kəˈlektəbl/ adj. 可收藏的
vocabulary.example: These vintage stamps are highly collectable.
vocabulary.translation: 这些复古邮票极具收藏价值。

vocabulary.entry: retro /ˈretrəʊ/ adj. 复古的；怀旧的
vocabulary.example: She decorated her room with retro furniture from the 1980s.
vocabulary.translation: 她用20世纪80年代的复古家具装饰房间。

sentences.english: Have you got any gadgets hanging around your home that you no longer want or use?
sentences.chinese: 你家里是不是堆着一些不再想要或使用的小电子产品？

sentences.chinese: 我们所有人的抽屉里，总共囤积着数百万件这类科技产品，而它们其实完全可以重获新生。

sentences.english: Part of the problem for our unloved gadgets is that many become obsolete quickly because their software doesn’t get updated.
sentences.chinese: 这些被我们闲置的电子产品之所以会被淘汰，部分原因是它们的软件无法更新，导致很快就过时了。

sentences.english: Other items are left unused because they’re broken or they’ve become superseded by a fancy new version.
sentences.chinese: 还有一些则是因为损坏，或是被更精致的新款产品取代而被束之高阁。

sentences.english: Many of these items are electronics, but despite them appearing to be past their sell-by date, they don’t need to end up in landfill.
sentences.chinese: 这些物品大多都属于电子产品，虽然看似已经毫无用处，但它们其实并不需要被扔进垃圾填埋场。

sentences.english: There are several ways to make the most of our unwanted gadgets.
sentences.chinese: 想要充分利用这些闲置电子产品，其实有好几种方法。

sentences.english: Recycling is the obvious solution.
sentences.chinese: 回收利用是最显而易见的一种。

sentences.english: Materials used to make them can be extracted and reused in other things.
sentences.chinese: 制造这些产品的原材料可以被提取出来，再用于其他物品的生产。

sentences.english: As an example, Elisabeth Ratcliffe from the Royal Society of Chemistry told the BBC: “There are about thirty different elements just in a smartphone, and many of them are very rare.”
sentences.chinese: 英国皇家化学会的伊丽莎白·拉特克利夫在接受BBC采访时举例说：“一部智能手机里就含有大约30种不同的元素，其中很多都是稀有元素。”

sentences.english: These can be used in touch screens and solar panels.
sentences.chinese: 这些元素可以用于制造触摸屏和太阳能电池板。

sentences.english: Probably the best antidote to our throwaway culture is to repair our broken tech.
sentences.chinese: 想要应对我们当下的“用完即弃”文化，最好的办法或许就是修理损坏的电子产品。

sentences.english: This takes patience and skill, which can be learnt at repair clubs and repair cafés – free meeting places where you’ll find tools and materials to help you make any repairs you need.
sentences.chinese: 这需要耐心和技巧，而这些都可以在修理俱乐部和修理咖啡馆里学到——这些免费的聚会场所会提供工具和材料，帮你完成所需的各类修理工作。

sentences.english: In the UK, the interest in mending our stuff and giving it a new life is reflected by the popularity of a TV series called The Repair Shop, where craftspeople rescue and resurrect items their owners thought were beyond saving.
sentences.chinese: 在英国，一档名为《修复店》的电视节目大受欢迎，这一现象也反映出人们对于修理物品、赋予其新生的浓厚兴趣。节目里的手工艺人会拯救并修复那些被主人认为已经无法挽救的物品。

sentences.english: A final option for your discarded gadgets is to upcycle them.
sentences.chinese: 处理废旧电子产品的最后一种办法是升级改造。

sentences.english: You can breathe new life into unwanted stuff by transforming it into valuable pieces or collectable retro items.
sentences.chinese: 你可以将这些闲置物品改造成有价值的物件或是具有收藏价值的复古单品，让它们重焕生机。

sentences.english: These could be sold on, meaning you can make some cash from your junk and create much needed space in your home!
sentences.chinese: 这些改造后的物品还可以拿去出售，这样你既能用“废品”赚点钱，又能为家里腾出急需的空间！

title: The weather of the future
paragraphs: As winter takes its icy grip, and we head outside into a cold and crisp morning, we might be dreaming of warmer and sunnier days that lie ahead. Although, for many, summer might give us the most clement weather, our changing climate might mean that our chilly winter season becomes a thing of the past. So maybe we should enjoy it while we can.

Last year, the World Meteorological Organization found that the Earth continued to endure a period of significant heating, making it one of the three hottest years on record. The most notable warmth was in the Siberian Arctic, where temperatures were 5°C above average. The evidence shows that much of this climate warming is driven by human activity.

With a shift in meteorological conditions, we’re likely to see more record-breaking temperatures, where, in certain places, summers will be scorching hot and winters mild. This means for some, snowy winters could become a thing of the past. In the UK, a series of projections, based on accelerating global emissions, found that the average coldest day would not drop below freezing point. Dr Lizzie Kendon, a senior Met Office scientist, told the BBC: “It could mean the end of sledging, snowmen and snowball fights… the overarching picture is warmer, wetter winters; hotter, drier summers.” She’s described this as ‘a wake-up call’.

Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is the obvious way to slow the rate of change in our climate. Some nations are promising to do this, but already we’re experiencing less snowfall and fewer frosty mornings. And on a bigger scale, glaciers are melting. According to modelling by Aberystwyth University in the UK, up to 92% of glaciers in the Alps could be lost by the end of the century due to climate change. So, if you’re lucky enough to be looking out on a winter wonderland, get outside and make the most of it before it melts.

vocabulary.entry: icy grip /ˈaɪsi ɡrɪp/ 寒气逼人；严寒的掌控
vocabulary.example: The town was in the icy grip of winter, with temperatures dropping below -10°C.
vocabulary.translation: 这座小镇被冬日的严寒笼罩，气温降至零下10摄氏度以下。

vocabulary.entry: crisp /krɪsp/ adj. （空气）清新凛冽的
vocabulary.example: We went for a walk on a crisp autumn morning.
vocabulary.translation: 我们在一个空气清新的秋日清晨出门散步。

vocabulary.entry: clement /ˈklemənt/ adj. （天气）温和宜人的
vocabulary.example: The region is known for its clement climate all year round.
vocabulary.translation: 该地区以全年温和宜人的气候而闻名。

vocabulary.entry: meteorological /ˌmiːtiərəˈlɒdʒɪkl/ adj. 气象的；气象学的
vocabulary.example: The meteorological department issued a storm warning yesterday.
vocabulary.translation: 气象部门昨天发布了暴雨预警。

vocabulary.entry: endure /ɪnˈdjʊə/ v. 持续经历；忍受
vocabulary.example: The city had to endure a week of heavy rain.
vocabulary.translation: 这座城市不得不经历一周的强降雨天气。

vocabulary.entry: significant heating /sɪɡˈnɪfɪkənt ˈhiːtɪŋ/ 显著升温
vocabulary.example: The data shows significant heating of the ocean surface over the past decade.
vocabulary.translation: 数据显示过去十年间海洋表面出现显著升温。

vocabulary.entry: on record /ɒn ˈrekɔːd/ 有记录以来的
vocabulary.example: Last month was the driest on record in this area.
vocabulary.translation: 上个月是该地区有记录以来最干旱的一个月。

vocabulary.entry: notable /ˈnəʊtəbl/ adj. 显著的；值得注意的
vocabulary.example: There was a notable improvement in her English after a year of study.
vocabulary.translation: 经过一年的学习，她的英语有了显著进步。

vocabulary.entry: drive /draɪv/ v. 驱动；促使
vocabulary.example: Technological innovation is driving the development of the industry.
vocabulary.translation: 技术创新正在推动这个行业的发展。

vocabulary.entry: shift /ʃɪft/ n. 转变；变化
vocabulary.example: There has been a noticeable shift in public opinion on this issue.
vocabulary.translation: 公众对这个问题的看法发生了明显转变。

vocabulary.entry: record-breaking /ˈrekɔːd ˌbreɪkɪŋ/ adj. 破纪录的
vocabulary.example: The athlete set a record-breaking time in the 100-metre race.
vocabulary.translation: 这位运动员在100米赛跑中创造了破纪录的成绩。

vocabulary.entry: scorching /ˈskɔːtʃɪŋ/ adj. 酷热的；灼热的
vocabulary.example: We stayed indoors during the scorching afternoon sun.
vocabulary.translation: 灼热的午后，我们一直待在室内。

vocabulary.entry: mild /maɪld/ adj. （天气）温和的
vocabulary.example: We had an unusually mild winter this year.
vocabulary.translation: 今年我们度过了一个异常温和的冬天。

vocabulary.entry: projection /prəˈdʒekʃn/ n. 预测；推测
vocabulary.example: The company's sales projection for next year is quite optimistic.
vocabulary.translation: 该公司对明年的销售额预测颇为乐观。

vocabulary.entry: accelerate /əkˈseləreɪt/ v. 加速；加快
vocabulary.example: The government plans to accelerate the pace of economic reform.
vocabulary.translation: 政府计划加快经济改革的步伐。

vocabulary.entry: freezing point /ˈfriːzɪŋ pɔɪnt/ 冰点
vocabulary.example: Water turns into ice when it reaches the freezing point.
vocabulary.translation: 水达到冰点时就会结冰。

vocabulary.entry: sledging /ˈsledʒɪŋ/ n. 滑雪橇运动
vocabulary.example: The children were excited about going sledging in the park.
vocabulary.translation: 孩子们对去公园滑雪橇感到兴奋不已。

vocabulary.entry: overarching /ˌəʊvəˈɑːtʃɪŋ/ adj. 总体的；全面的
vocabulary.example: The overarching goal of the project is to reduce poverty.
vocabulary.translation: 这个项目的总体目标是减少贫困。

vocabulary.entry: wake-up call /ˈweɪk ʌp kɔːl/ 警钟；警示
vocabulary.example: The recent accident is a wake-up call for all factories to improve safety.
vocabulary.translation: 最近的这场事故给所有工厂敲响了加强安全管理的警钟。

vocabulary.entry: greenhouse gas /ˈɡriːnhaʊs ɡæs/ 温室气体
vocabulary.example: Carbon dioxide is one of the main greenhouse gases.
vocabulary.translation: 二氧化碳是主要的温室气体之一。

vocabulary.entry: emission /ɪˈmɪʃn/ n. 排放物；排放
vocabulary.example: The factory has reduced its carbon emissions by 30% this year.
vocabulary.translation: 这家工厂今年的碳排放量减少了30%。

vocabulary.entry: frosty /ˈfrɒsti/ adj. 结霜的；严寒的
vocabulary.example: The garden was covered with frosty grass in the morning.
vocabulary.translation: 清晨，花园里的草上结满了白霜。

vocabulary.entry: glacier /ˈɡlæsiə/ n. 冰川
vocabulary.example: The glacier has been melting at an alarming rate in recent years.
vocabulary.translation: 近年来，这座冰川的消融速度令人担忧。

vocabulary.entry: modelling /ˈmɒdəlɪŋ/ n. 建模；模型研究
vocabulary.example: Computer modelling helps scientists predict climate change.
vocabulary.translation: 计算机建模帮助科学家预测气候变化。

vocabulary.entry: winter wonderland /ˈwɪntə ˈwʌndəlænd/ 冬日仙境；银装素裹的景致
vocabulary.example: After the heavy snow, the town turned into a beautiful winter wonderland.
vocabulary.translation: 大雪过后，这座小镇变成了一个美丽的冬日仙境。

sentences.english: As winter takes its icy grip, and we head outside into a cold and crisp morning, we might be dreaming of warmer and sunnier days that lie ahead.
sentences.chinese: 当冬天寒气逼人，我们顶着凛冽清新的晨风出门时，心里或许会憧憬着即将到来的温暖艳阳天。

sentences.english: Although, for many, summer might give us the most clement weather, our changing climate might mean that our chilly winter season becomes a thing of the past.
sentences.chinese: 对很多人来说，夏天的天气或许最为宜人，但气候变化可能会让寒冷的冬季成为历史。

sentences.english: So maybe we should enjoy it while we can.
sentences.chinese: 所以，或许我们该趁还能享受冬日，好好珍惜它。

sentences.english: Last year, the World Meteorological Organization found that the Earth continued to endure a period of significant heating, making it one of the three hottest years on record.
sentences.chinese: 去年，世界气象组织发现，地球仍处于显著升温阶段，去年也因此成为有记录以来最热的三个年份之一。

sentences.english: The most notable warmth was in the Siberian Arctic, where temperatures were 5°C above average.
sentences.chinese: 升温现象最明显的区域是西伯利亚北极地区，当地气温比平均值高出了5摄氏度。

sentences.english: The evidence shows that much of this climate warming is driven by human activity.
sentences.chinese: 有证据表明，气候变暖在很大程度上是由人类活动导致的。

sentences.english: With a shift in meteorological conditions, we’re likely to see more record-breaking temperatures, where, in certain places, summers will be scorching hot and winters mild.
sentences.chinese: 随着气象条件的转变，我们可能会迎来更多破纪录的气温，部分地区会出现夏季酷暑难耐、冬季温暖和煦的情况。

sentences.english: This means for some, snowy winters could become a thing of the past.
sentences.chinese: 这意味着对一些地方来说，飘雪的冬天可能会成为历史。

sentences.english: In the UK, a series of projections, based on accelerating global emissions, found that the average coldest day would not drop below freezing point.
sentences.chinese: 在英国，一系列基于全球排放加速增长的预测显示，当地最冷日子的平均气温将不会跌破冰点。

sentences.english: Dr Lizzie Kendon, a senior Met Office scientist, told the BBC: “It could mean the end of sledging, snowmen and snowball fights… the overarching picture is warmer, wetter winters; hotter, drier summers.”
sentences.chinese: 英国气象局资深科学家莉齐·肯顿博士在接受BBC采访时表示：“这可能意味着滑雪橇、堆雪人、打雪仗这些活动将成为历史……总体趋势就是冬季变得更暖更湿，夏季变得更热更干。”

sentences.english: She’s described this as ‘a wake-up call’.
sentences.chinese: 她将这种情况称为一次“警钟”。

sentences.english: Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is the obvious way to slow the rate of change in our climate.
sentences.chinese: 减少温室气体排放是减缓气候变化速度的有效途径。

sentences.english: Some nations are promising to do this, but already we’re experiencing less snowfall and fewer frosty mornings.
sentences.chinese: 一些国家已承诺会采取相关措施，但我们已经在经历降雪量减少、霜冻清晨变少的状况。

sentences.english: And on a bigger scale, glaciers are melting.
sentences.chinese: 从更大范围来看，冰川也在不断消融。

sentences.english: According to modelling by Aberystwyth University in the UK, up to 92% of glaciers in the Alps could be lost by the end of the century due to climate change.
sentences.chinese: 英国阿伯里斯特威斯大学的模型研究显示，到本世纪末，气候变化可能会导致阿尔卑斯山高达92%的冰川消失。

sentences.english: So, if you’re lucky enough to be looking out on a winter wonderland, get outside and make the most of it before it melts.
sentences.chinese: 所以，如果你有幸能看到银装素裹的冬日美景，一定要出门去，在它消融前好好享受这份景致。

title: Clever trees
paragraphs: There’s nothing better than a walk in the countryside for lifting our spirits. Connecting with nature has been proven to help our mental health. For some, the best tonic is to stroll through a forest, but as we admire the trees that surround us, it’s worth knowing these trees are doing more than just being nice things to look at.

We’re already aware of the healing properties of trees – they produce oxygen and clean the air we breathe by absorbing about a quarter of all human-caused carbon dioxide emissions. Deforestation isn’t helping with this which is why so many people want to save them. But there’s more to these impressive forms of vegetation than we might think. Researchers have discovered evidence that proves they are actually intelligent.

It’s thought that trees talk and share resources right under our feet, using a fungal network. Under the ground are tree roots, and mingling among them, along with bacteria, are thousands of superfine threads of fungi, known as hyphae. And research has shown that they are all interconnected. They can help each other by sharing nutrients, and they can even warn of approaching threats. Scientists say it’s like the trees are talking to one another.

Ecologist Suzanne Simard has called this network the Wood Wide Web. She discovered that parent trees use this network to help their offspring. Speaking to the BBC, she said: “We found that the parent trees would favour those seedlings that were of their own kin versus the strangers” by sending them more nutrients. She also found that trees are smart enough to change their behaviour and have managed to adapt and survive in a changing environment.
So it seems trees really are the stars of our natural world, and with around three trillion of them on our planet, it’s time to show them some respect if we want them to flourish.

vocabulary.entry: root /ruːt/ n. 根；根部

vocabulary.entry: hypha /ˈhaɪfə/ n. 菌丝（单数）

vocabulary.translation: 菌丝是真菌的营养器官之一。

vocabulary.entry: offspring /ˈɒfsprɪŋ/ n. 后代；子孙

vocabulary.entry: favour /ˈfeɪvə/ v. 偏爱；偏袒

sentences.english: So it seems trees really are the stars of our natural world, and with around three trillion of them on our planet, it’s time to show them some respect if we want them to flourish.

title: Blue Monday
paragraphs: Ask most people which day of the week they dread the most and the answer is likely to be Monday. The first day of the week can make us grouchy and depressed, which is why the feeling is described as the Monday blues. But what is it exactly that makes us feel down and does it affect everyone?

Apparently, the most depressing day of the year is the third Monday in January, when it’s cold and dark outside. This day was nicknamed ‘Blue Monday’ by psychologist Cliff Arnall in 2004. He came up with it after a holiday company asked him for a ‘scientific formula’ for the January blues.

Even if there was little science behind the formula, it’s probably true that the sound of our alarm clock on any Monday morning signals the dawning of a new week and possibly the end of our weekend of fun. Research shows our Monday mood can be based on a direct comparison to the day before. It’s what psychologists call an emotional shift, and no other part of the week has a transition like it.

Monday means the end of weekend lie-ins – it’s back to the routine and the realisation that there are five days ahead of the nine-to-five, and according to the BBC Bitesize website “If you can’t stand your job then the Monday blues can be very real.” And your miserable Monday is followed by trying Tuesday – the most popular day for sending out job applications.

But is Monday as bad as we like to think it is? Feeling a bit low shouldn’t be confused with more serious depression, caused by other factors. Writing for the BBC, author and presenter Claudia Hammond, argues that this low feeling might be a myth. She says: “There is a strong cultural idea that we don’t like Mondays.” She mentions an Australian study in 2008 about how people reflected on their mood and found the day that scored the lowest was in fact Wednesdays. So, when Monday comes, maybe we should give it a second chance!

vocabulary.entry: dread /dred/ v. 害怕；畏惧
vocabulary.example: She dreads having to speak in public.
vocabulary.translation: 她害怕当众发言。

vocabulary.entry: grouchy /ˈɡraʊtʃi/ adj. 脾气暴躁的；烦躁的
vocabulary.example: He's always grouchy in the morning until he's had his coffee.
vocabulary.translation: 他早上喝完咖啡之前总是很烦躁。

vocabulary.entry: Monday blues /ˈmʌndi bluːz/ n. 周一忧郁症
vocabulary.example: Many people suffer from the Monday blues at the start of the working week.
vocabulary.translation: 很多人在新一周工作开始时都会患上周一忧郁症。

vocabulary.entry: depressing /dɪˈpresɪŋ/ adj. 令人沮丧的；让人消沉的
vocabulary.example: The news from the war zone is deeply depressing.
vocabulary.translation: 来自战区的消息实在令人沮丧。

vocabulary.entry: nickname /ˈnɪkneɪm/ v. 给……起绰号；把……称为
vocabulary.example: The locals nicknamed the old building 'The Grey Lady'.
vocabulary.translation: 当地人把这座老建筑戏称为“灰色夫人”。

vocabulary.entry: Blue Monday /bluː ˈmʌndi/ n. 蓝色星期一（指一年中最沮丧的一天）
vocabulary.example: Blue Monday is said to be the third Monday in January.
vocabulary.translation: 蓝色星期一被认为是每年一月的第三个周一。

vocabulary.entry: scientific formula /ˌsaɪənˈtɪfɪk ˈfɔːmjələ/ n. 科学公式
vocabulary.example: The student tried to work out the scientific formula for the chemical reaction.
vocabulary.translation: 这个学生试图推算出这个化学反应的科学公式。

vocabulary.entry: January blues /ˈdʒænjuəri bluːz/ n. 一月忧郁症
vocabulary.example: The January blues often affect people who dislike cold and dark weather.
vocabulary.translation: 一月忧郁症常常会影响那些讨厌阴冷天气的人。

vocabulary.entry: alarm clock /əˈlɑːm klɒk/ n. 闹钟
vocabulary.example: I set my alarm clock for 6 a.m. to catch the early train.
vocabulary.translation: 我把闹钟定在早上六点，好赶上早班火车。

vocabulary.entry: signal /ˈsɪɡnəl/ v. 标志着；表明
vocabulary.example: The bell signals the end of the class.
vocabulary.translation: 铃声标志着这节课的结束。

vocabulary.entry: dawning /ˈdɔːnɪŋ/ n. 开端；起始
vocabulary.example: We are at the dawning of a new era in technology.
vocabulary.translation: 我们正处在一个科技新纪元的开端。

vocabulary.entry: emotional shift /ɪˈməʊʃənl ʃɪft/ n. 情绪转变
vocabulary.example: The emotional shift from excitement to sadness happened very quickly.
vocabulary.translation: 从兴奋到悲伤的情绪转变发生得非常快。

vocabulary.entry: transition /trænˈzɪʃn/ n. 过渡；转变
vocabulary.example: The transition from childhood to adulthood can be difficult.
vocabulary.translation: 从童年到成年的过渡可能会很艰难。

vocabulary.entry: lie-in /ˈlaɪ ɪn/ n. 懒觉；睡过头
vocabulary.example: I love having a lie-in on Sunday mornings.
vocabulary.translation: 我喜欢在周日早上睡个懒觉。

vocabulary.entry: routine /ruːˈtiːn/ n. 常规；惯例
vocabulary.example: I need to get back into my exercise routine after the holiday.
vocabulary.translation: 假期过后，我需要重新恢复锻炼的习惯。

vocabulary.entry: nine-to-five /ˌnaɪn tə ˈfaɪv/ n. 朝九晚五的工作
vocabulary.example: She's tired of her boring nine-to-five job.
vocabulary.translation: 她厌倦了自己那份枯燥的朝九晚五的工作。

vocabulary.entry: can’t stand /kænt stænd/ 无法忍受
vocabulary.example: I can't stand the noise from the construction site next door.
vocabulary.translation: 我无法忍受隔壁建筑工地的噪音。

vocabulary.entry: miserable /ˈmɪzrəbl/ adj. 令人不快的；糟糕的
vocabulary.example: We had a miserable time on the camping trip because it rained nonstop.
vocabulary.translation: 我们的露营之旅很糟糕，因为雨一直下个不停。

vocabulary.entry: trying /ˈtraɪɪŋ/ adj. 令人难受的；费劲的
vocabulary.example: It was a trying day with one problem after another.
vocabulary.translation: 那真是难熬的一天，麻烦事一件接着一件。

vocabulary.entry: job application /dʒɒb ˌæplɪˈkeɪʃn/ n. 求职申请
vocabulary.example: He spent the evening filling out job applications online.
vocabulary.translation: 他花了一整晚在网上填写求职申请表。

sentences.english: Ask most people which day of the week they dread the most and the answer is likely to be Monday.
sentences.chinese: 问大多数人一周中最害怕哪一天，答案很可能是周一。

sentences.english: The first day of the week can make us grouchy and depressed, which is why the feeling is described as the Monday blues.
sentences.chinese: 一周的第一天总会让我们变得烦躁又低落，这种情绪也因此被称为“周一忧郁症”。

sentences.english: But what is it exactly that makes us feel down and does it affect everyone?
sentences.chinese: 但究竟是什么让我们心情变差，这种情绪又会影响每一个人吗？

sentences.english: Apparently, the most depressing day of the year is the third Monday in January, when it’s cold and dark outside.
sentences.chinese: 显然，一年中最让人沮丧的日子是一月的第三个周一，彼时室外天寒地冻、昼短夜长。

sentences.english: This day was nicknamed ‘Blue Monday’ by psychologist Cliff Arnall in 2004.
sentences.chinese: 心理学家克利夫·阿诺尔在2004年将这一天命名为“蓝色星期一”。

sentences.english: He came up with it after a holiday company asked him for a ‘scientific formula’ for the January blues.
sentences.chinese: 当时一家度假公司请他推算出一个解释“一月忧郁症”的“科学公式”，这个说法便由此诞生。

sentences.english: Even if there was little science behind the formula, it’s probably true that the sound of our alarm clock on any Monday morning signals the dawning of a new week and possibly the end of our weekend of fun.
sentences.chinese: 尽管这个公式并没有太多科学依据，但有一点或许是事实：每个周一清晨的闹钟声，都意味着新一周的开始，也可能宣告着充满乐趣的周末就此结束。

sentences.english: Research shows our Monday mood can be based on a direct comparison to the day before.
sentences.chinese: 研究表明，我们周一的心情好坏，往往源于与前一天的直接对比。

sentences.english: It’s what psychologists call an emotional shift, and no other part of the week has a transition like it.
sentences.chinese: 这就是心理学家所说的“情绪转变”，一周之中再也没有哪个时段会有如此强烈的状态切换。

sentences.english: Monday means the end of weekend lie-ins – it’s back to the routine and the realisation that there are five days ahead of the nine-to-five, and according to the BBC Bitesize website “If you can’t stand your job then the Monday blues can be very real.”
sentences.chinese: 周一意味着周末懒觉的终结——大家要重新回归日常工作生活，同时意识到朝九晚五的日子还要持续五天。英国广播公司教学科普网站BBC Bitesize提到：“如果你无法忍受自己的工作，那么周一忧郁症就会真实地找上门来。”

sentences.english: And your miserable Monday is followed by trying Tuesday – the most popular day for sending out job applications.
sentences.chinese: 在令人郁闷的周一过后，接踵而至的是“求职周二”——这一天是人们投递求职信的高峰期。

sentences.english: But is Monday as bad as we like to think it is?
sentences.chinese: 但周一真的像我们想象中那么糟糕吗？

sentences.english: Feeling a bit low shouldn’t be confused with more serious depression, caused by other factors.
sentences.chinese: 这种轻微的低落情绪，不应与由其他因素引发的更为严重的抑郁症混为一谈。

sentences.english: Writing for the BBC, author and presenter Claudia Hammond, argues that this low feeling might be a myth.
sentences.chinese: 作家兼主持人克劳迪娅·哈蒙德在为BBC撰写的文章中指出，这种对周一的抵触感可能只是一种错误的固有印象。

sentences.english: She says: “There is a strong cultural idea that we don’t like Mondays.”
sentences.chinese: 她表示：“不喜欢周一已经成了一种根深蒂固的文化观念。”

sentences.english: She mentions an Australian study in 2008 about how people reflected on their mood and found the day that scored the lowest was in fact Wednesdays.
sentences.chinese: 她还提到2008年澳大利亚的一项研究，该研究调查了人们对自身情绪的回顾，结果发现情绪最低落的日子其实是周三。

sentences.english: So, when Monday comes, maybe we should give it a second chance!
sentences.chinese: 所以，当周一来临时，或许我们应该再给它一次机会！

title: Language-learning apps
titleChinese: 用语言学习应用软件学外语
paragraphs: Are you learning another language? Maybe you’re trying to get to grips with it for work or study, or maybe you’re trying to master it just for the fun of it? Language learning is nothing new, of course, but technology has made it easier than ever to grasp.

The popularity of language-learning apps in particular has boomed around the world, especially as more people are working or studying at home. They are usually easy and convenient to use because you can access them on your smartphone. And apps can offer languages not popular enough to be taught at evening classes or schools or universities.

Many of us are aiming to be bilingual to enable us to communicate with people around the world. But, maybe surprisingly, it’s the British, who are not renowned for their enthusiasm for language learning, who are leading the way in the growth of these apps. US firm Duolingo told the BBC that in 2020 new user numbers globally were up 67% compared with 2019, while in the UK they shot up by 132%, almost double the worldwide average. And London-based Busuu, saw a similar trend for learners based in the UK.

But for anyone trying their hand at a new language, what motivates them to carry on learning when there isn’t a teacher around to manage their progress? Colin Watkins from Duolingo told the BBC that for UK learners at least, “people are learning because of culture, brain training, family, and relationships, along with school and travel. We want a positive use of our time, and to do something productive on our phones.” The recent lockdowns have given us more time to do this. Certainly, becoming bilingual or a polyglot is a good thing, and it helps us to bring the world a little closer together.

title: Texting or talking
paragraphs: The telephone was an amazing invention. People could finally speak to each other instantly from one home to another. The mobile phone took this technology further, meaning we could make contact with people to and from almost anywhere in the world. But despite having the instant ability to talk to one another, it seems many of us prefer to communicate by text.

I don’t mean we have taken up letter writing again. Although a handwritten letter has a personal touch, sending it by snail mail is too slow to satisfy our desire to keep in touch immediately. But what our smartphones now allow us to do is enable us to communicate in any number of quick, cheap but silent ways. A study in the UK a few years ago found 49 per cent of teenagers preferred to send a text rather than speak to someone.

Certainly sending an SMS, text or message via a chat app means we can compose what we want to say, and we can be more efficient in saying it – especially if we express ourselves by using emojis. It can also be quicker than having to chat with someone, although I feel you can still end up wasting time by having a full discussion by text! Text messaging also allows privacy – other people can’t overhear your text if you’re in a public place such as on a train.

But texting instead of talking can seem antisocial; we may even forget the art of pleasantries. A text can be misinterpreted too because you miss out on a speaker’s intonation. Neuroscientist Professor Sophie Scott told the BBC: “We always speak with melody and intonation to our voice… you take that channel of information out of communication, you lose another way that sense is being conveyed.”
Of course texting and talking is the worst thing to do. Who deserves your attention when two people are communicating with you? It’s then we have to decide who has the most interesting thing to say!

sentences.english: The telephone was an amazing invention.
sentences.chinese: 电话是一项了不起的发明。

sentences.english: People could finally speak to each other instantly from one home to another.
sentences.chinese: 人们终于能够足不出户，即刻与彼此对话。

sentences.english: The mobile phone took this technology further, meaning we could make contact with people to and from almost anywhere in the world.
sentences.chinese: 移动电话则将这项技术推向了新高度，这意味着我们几乎能与世界各地的人随时取得联系。

sentences.english: But despite having the instant ability to talk to one another, it seems many of us prefer to communicate by text.
sentences.chinese: 但即便拥有了即时通话的能力，我们中的许多人似乎还是更偏爱用短信沟通。

sentences.english: I don’t mean we have taken up letter writing again.
sentences.chinese: 我并不是说大家又重拾了写信的习惯。

sentences.english: Although a handwritten letter has a personal touch, sending it by snail mail is too slow to satisfy our desire to keep in touch immediately.
sentences.chinese: 虽说手写信件带有独特的个人温度，但平信邮寄的方式实在太慢，满足不了我们即时联络的需求。

sentences.english: But what our smartphones now allow us to do is enable us to communicate in any number of quick, cheap but silent ways.
sentences.chinese: 而智能手机如今能让我们通过多种多样快捷、廉价又安静的方式进行沟通。

sentences.english: A study in the UK a few years ago found 49 per cent of teenagers preferred to send a text rather than speak to someone.
sentences.chinese: 英国几年前的一项研究显示，49%的青少年更喜欢发短信，而非直接与人交谈。

sentences.english: Certainly sending an SMS, text or message via a chat app means we can compose what we want to say, and we can be more efficient in saying it – especially if we express ourselves by using emojis.
sentences.chinese: 毫无疑问，通过短信、文字消息或是聊天软件发送信息，能让我们斟酌好想要说的话，并且更高效地表达——尤其是当我们用表情符号辅助表达时。

sentences.english: It can also be quicker than having to chat with someone, although I feel you can still end up wasting time by having a full discussion by text!
sentences.chinese: 这种方式通常也比实时通话更省时，不过我觉得，要是用短信来展开一次完整的讨论，最终还是会耗费不少时间！

sentences.english: Text messaging also allows privacy – other people can’t overhear your text if you’re in a public place such as on a train.
sentences.chinese: 短信沟通还能保障隐私——当你身处火车之类的公共场所时，旁人不会听到你的聊天内容。

sentences.english: But texting instead of talking can seem antisocial; we may even forget the art of pleasantries.
sentences.chinese: 但只发短信不与人交谈，会显得有些不合群，我们甚至可能会忘掉寒暄的社交艺术。

sentences.english: A text can be misinterpreted too because you miss out on a speaker’s intonation.
sentences.chinese: 短信内容也很容易被误解，因为你无法捕捉到说话人的语调。

sentences.english: Neuroscientist Professor Sophie Scott told the BBC: “We always speak with melody and intonation to our voice… you take that channel of information out of communication, you lose another way that sense is being conveyed.”
sentences.chinese: 神经科学家索菲·斯科特教授在接受BBC采访时表示：“我们说话时，声音里总会带有抑扬顿挫的语调……如果在沟通中去掉了这一信息传递渠道，就等于失去了另一种表达语义的方式。”

sentences.english: Of course texting and talking is the worst thing to do.
sentences.chinese: 当然，一边发短信一边打电话是最不可取的行为。

sentences.english: Who deserves your attention when two people are communicating with you?
sentences.chinese: 当两个人同时在和你沟通时，你该把注意力放在谁身上呢？

sentences.english: It’s then we have to decide who has the most interesting thing to say!
sentences.chinese: 到那时，你就得判断出谁的话更有意思了！

title: The benefits of spring cleaning
paragraphs: You may well have heard of the term ‘spring cleaning’: the act of giving your house a deep clean in the spring months. Even though, for many of us, that ritual of a once-a-year blitz of dirt and grime is dying out, some of us still practise it. However, there could be a good reason the tradition isn’t as popular as it was.

The spring months are associated with new life and warmth – a stark contrast to the cold, gloomy winter that preceded. For protection against the freezing weather outside, people would seal their doors and windows as best they could to keep the heat in. In a time when many houses had fireplaces, open fires would churn out smoke and soot, coating rooms with layers of muck and gunk.

It therefore made sense for people to start cleaning in the spring, when the weather was warmer and windows opened, to freshen up their houses, swabbing the floors and cleaning the walls. However, open fires are no longer commonplace in modern British homes, with people preferring central heating to filthy smoke. And it’s not just the way of heating our homes that has changed. In the past, cleaning was designated to specific times and days, as simple chores like washing clothes took a long time. The rise of gadgets such as the washing machine means that tasks are quicker and more efficient.

However, psychologists such as Dr Jonathan Fader, argue that the mental health benefits of clearing the house of mess means that a spring clean is hugely positive. The perception of your house being cluttered can cause the stress hormone cortisol to rise.

So, while the tradition is still there, and it’s nice to have a big purge of dirt once in a while, it is no longer as necessary – or limited to just the spring. That said, the psychological benefits of having a tidy home means that a once-a-year purge of unnecessary items, rather than dirt, can make you feel much better.

title: The life of a pro-gamer
titleChinese: 职业游戏玩家的生活是什么样的？
paragraphs: From pixel representations of table tennis in the 1970s to modern day cinematic storytelling, video games have evolved a lot and become more immersive. But it’s not just the graphics and gameplay mechanics that have changed – it has also opened up a range of career options, including that of professional gamer.

When gaming first started, those who loved video games and wanted to make a career out of them often ended up as developers, testers or coders. While there were competitions, sometimes held worldwide, in which amateur gamers could win money or prizes, it wasn’t really considered a career path until the late 2000s, when live streaming really took off and gamers became celebrities.

With e-sports now an integral part of gaming, what does a professional gamer’s life look like? The key, according to many pro-gamers, is practice – the same with many sports. While choosing the best peripherals is important, such as the right controller or keyboard, most pro-gamers spend hours every day working out hacks to save time or improve their chances of winning. And it’s not just while playing games that they need to be active, but also in real life. Exercising and stretching is vital to avoid injuries to their backs and wrists and preventing eye fatigue from spending long hours staring at monitors by taking regular screen breaks.

But it’s not just the physical aspects that gamers need to be careful with. According to some experts, like Dr Phil Birch, while the physical demands of e-sports and traditional sports are very different, the psychological impacts can be similar: regulating emotions, dealing with pressure and big crowds, and overcoming injury are just some of the common factors.
So, while the life of a pro-gamer may sound fun with lots of button bashing, just remember that it takes a lot of discipline and hard work to do it full-time.

vocabulary.entry: take off /teɪk ɒf/ （事业等）腾飞；突然成功
vocabulary.example: The e-sports industry really took off in the early 2010s.
vocabulary.translation: 电竞行业在21世纪10年代初真正迎来了腾飞。

vocabulary.entry: e-sports /ˈiː spɔːts/ n. 电子竞技

vocabulary.translation: 一款高品质的外设能够提升电竞选手的表现。

vocabulary.entry: controller /kənˈtrəʊlə/ n. （游戏）手柄

vocabulary.translation: 他买了一台高刷新率显示器，以获得更流畅的游戏体验。

vocabulary.entry: screen break /skriːn breɪk/ 屏幕休息时间

title: Is this year shorter than normal 2021
paragraphs: ‘Time waits for no man’ – or so the saying goes. We can’t stop time and we can’t control it, although sometimes, in our minds, we think time flies – for example, when the weekend arrives, we feel it’s over in no time! But if this year in particular feels like it’s passing more quickly than others have done, there could be a scientific explanation why.

Of course, we know a year is usually 365 days long. Clever scientists calculated this a long time ago. They also worked out that every four years, we need an extra day to keep our calendar in sync – this is called a leap year. But 2021 isn’t one of those years, and yet it’s not behaving like a normal year. Scientists and astrophysicists have done the math and discovered the Earth is moving faster than it ever has in the last 50 years. This means that 2021 is going to be the shortest year in decades.

Apparently, this is because the Earth is spinning faster on its axis, quicker than it has done in decades, and the days are therefore shorter. But they are only short by a tiny amount – around 0.05 milliseconds – so don’t panic if you haven’t noticed! However, long-term these milliseconds add up. Astrophysicist Graham Jones and Konstantin Bikos from Time and Date told The Independent newspaper: “If the Earth’s rotation continues to quicken, we may at some point require a negative leap second. If this happens, our clocks would skip a second in order to keep up with the hurrying Earth.” Since 1972, 27 leap seconds have only been added to our time and none have been taken away.

This really is only of concern for atomic clocks – the most accurate timekeeping devices in history. Studying the Earth’s rotation and then subtracting or adding a leap second to these clocks can ensure they remain aligned and keep us on time. But now, maybe we need to get a move on before this ‘shorter’ year is gone in a split second!

title: Cooking and mental health
titleChinese: 烹饪对心理健康的影响
paragraphs: ‘We are what we eat’ – or so the saying goes. From calorie-inducing meals to low-fat lunches, much of our health depends on what we eat. We know about the benefits of eating properly for our physical wellbeing, but food – and cooking it – is proving to be good for our mental wellbeing as well.

Some people are now advocating the therapeutic value of cooking food. It’s not just about the end result but the experience someone goes through. Dr Mark Salter, a consultant psychiatrist, told the BBC: “Baking and cooking are good occupational therapies that help patients develop planning skills, short-term memory and social skills – all of which suffer in mental illness.”

TV chef and author Nadiya Hussain agrees that cooking is great for helping our mind. She loves to bake and became the champion of the TV show, The Great British Bake Off. She says that “Baking’s always been about therapy... It’s never really been about the cake.” And she thinks that baking is an important tool for our socialisation and mental health.

Certainly, creating some delicious food has helped some of us get through the recent lockdown; it’s helped take our mind off things and given us something to do. People have said that kneading dough to make bread, for example, has given them a sense of calm and control. Research has shown that doing creative tasks, like cooking, makes us feel happier. Nicole Farmer, who studies how food impacts our biology, behaviour and mental health, told BBC online that “cooking represents the shared human experience of food, and nurturing people through food, so I think that’s where it incorporates opportunity for immediate positive emotions.”

Of course, cooking can be a very sociable activity and sharing the end result, a rewarding experience. Hopefully, as we start to mix with friends and family again, we can enjoy the benefits once more and put us all in the right frame of mind.

vocabulary.translation: 那天我没处在适合做决定的心态中。

vocabulary.entry: advocate /ˈædvəkeɪt/ v. 倡导；拥护

vocabulary.entry: wellbeing /ˈwelbiːɪŋ/ n. 健康；幸福
vocabulary.example: Regular exercise is essential for physical and mental wellbeing.
vocabulary.translation: 规律运动对身心健康至关重要。

vocabulary.entry: champion /ˈtʃæmpiən/ n. 冠军
vocabulary.example: She became the champion of the tennis tournament last year.
vocabulary.translation: 她去年夺得网球锦标赛的冠军。

vocabulary.entry: impact /ˈɪmpækt/ v. 影响
vocabulary.example: Climate change can impact the growth of crops significantly.
vocabulary.translation: 气候变化会对农作物的生长产生显著影响。

vocabulary.entry: shared experience /ʃeəd ɪkˈspɪəriəns/ 共同体验
vocabulary.example: Celebrating festivals is a shared experience for the whole family.
vocabulary.translation: 庆祝节日是全家人的共同体验。

vocabulary.entry: lockdown /ˈlɒkdaʊn/ n. 封锁；管控
vocabulary.example: The city announced a lockdown to control the spread of the virus.
vocabulary.translation: 这座城市宣布实施封锁，以控制病毒的传播。

sentences.english: ‘We are what we eat’ – or so the saying goes.
sentences.chinese: 常言道，“人如其食”。

sentences.english: From calorie-inducing meals to low-fat lunches, much of our health depends on what we eat.
sentences.chinese: 从容易摄入过量卡路里的大餐，到低脂午餐，我们的健康很大程度上取决于日常饮食。

sentences.english: We know about the benefits of eating properly for our physical wellbeing, but food – and cooking it – is proving to be good for our mental wellbeing as well.
sentences.chinese: 我们都清楚合理膳食对身体健康的益处，但事实证明，食物本身以及烹饪的过程，对心理健康同样大有裨益。

sentences.english: Some people are now advocating the therapeutic value of cooking food.
sentences.chinese: 如今有人开始倡导烹饪所具有的治疗价值。

sentences.english: It’s not just about the end result but the experience someone goes through.
sentences.chinese: 这种价值不只体现在最终的成品上，更蕴藏在烹饪的全过程之中。

sentences.english: Dr Mark Salter, a consultant psychiatrist, told the BBC: “Baking and cooking are good occupational therapies that help patients develop planning skills, short-term memory and social skills – all of which suffer in mental illness.”
sentences.chinese: 高级顾问精神病学家马克·索尔特博士在接受BBC采访时表示：“烘焙和烹饪是极佳的职业疗法，能帮助患者培养规划能力、短时记忆力以及社交能力——而这些能力在患上精神疾病后都会受到损害。”

sentences.english: TV chef and author Nadiya Hussain agrees that cooking is great for helping our mind.
sentences.chinese: 电视主厨兼作家娜迪亚·侯赛因也认同烹饪对改善心理状态有显著作用。

sentences.english: She loves to bake and became the champion of the TV show, The Great British Bake Off.
sentences.chinese: 她热爱烘焙，还曾夺得电视节目《英国家庭烘焙大赛》的冠军。

sentences.english: She says that “Baking’s always been about therapy... It’s never really been about the cake.”
sentences.chinese: 她表示：“烘焙从来都与疗愈相关……蛋糕本身从来都不是核心。”

sentences.english: And she thinks that baking is an important tool for our socialisation and mental health.
sentences.chinese: 在她看来，烘焙是帮助人们实现社交、维护心理健康的重要方式。

sentences.english: Certainly, creating some delicious food has helped some of us get through the recent lockdown; it’s helped take our mind off things and given us something to do.
sentences.chinese: 诚然，制作美味的食物帮助许多人熬过了此前的封锁期，它能帮我们转移注意力，也能让我们的生活有所寄托。

sentences.english: People have said that kneading dough to make bread, for example, has given them a sense of calm and control.
sentences.chinese: 比如有人说，揉面团做面包的过程，能让他们获得内心的平静和一种掌控感。

sentences.english: Research has shown that doing creative tasks, like cooking, makes us feel happier.
sentences.chinese: 研究表明，从事烹饪这类创造性活动，能让我们感到更愉悦。

sentences.english: Nicole Farmer, who studies how food impacts our biology, behaviour and mental health, told BBC online that “cooking represents the shared human experience of food, and nurturing people through food, so I think that’s where it incorporates opportunity for immediate positive emotions.”
sentences.chinese: 研究食物对人体生理机能、行为举止以及心理健康影响的妮可·法默在接受BBC在线采访时表示：“烹饪象征着人类共通的饮食体验，也是通过食物去滋养他人的过程，我认为这正是它能带来即时积极情绪的原因所在。”

sentences.english: Of course, cooking can be a very sociable activity and sharing the end result, a rewarding experience.
sentences.chinese: 当然，烹饪本身就是一项极具社交属性的活动，分享烹饪成果更是一种能带来成就感的体验。

sentences.english: Hopefully, as we start to mix with friends and family again, we can enjoy the benefits once more and put us all in the right frame of mind.
sentences.chinese: 希望随着我们重新与亲友相聚，能再次享受烹饪带来的种种益处，让每个人都拥有良好的精神状态。

title: How to create good habits
paragraphs: Have you ever made a promise to yourself that you didn’t keep? Commonly, when the new year ticks over, we make resolutions: going to the gym, studying harder or giving up a bad habit. Sadly, not long after we’ve made the promise, we often end up breaking them. But what if you want to create a new good habit? Well, it’s possible, but willpower might not be the only thing you need.

The basic idea of a habit is something we do almost unconsciously, as if you’re on autopilot. An example of this would be having breakfast or saying ‘please’ and ‘thank you’. Good habits can be part of your daily routine. But if we don’t have those habits, how can we create them? According to a study published by the European Journal of Social Psychology, it takes an average of 66 days to form a new habit. However, relying only on determination may not be the answer.

Questioning why you want something to be the norm rather than relying on your resolve could be the key. Do you want to lose weight because you want to be healthier or feel more attractive? The issue is, willpower could be subject to your mood – a bad mood may mean you don’t want to do something.

You should also avoid trying to change too much at once – remember that it’s a case of baby steps. Giving up all your favourite foods, going to the gym, and stopping drinking at the same time will probably result in failure rather than sustainable practice. And don’t worry about failing – just start again!

Finally, don’t do things outside your comfort zone. If you hate mushrooms, don’t persevere and try to add them to your diet just to be healthier. Eat something you like! It might not be quick, but if you follow these tips, you may be able to change something for the better or kick a bad habit.

vocabulary.entry: baby step /ˈbeɪbi step/ n. 一小步；循序渐进的步骤

vocabulary.translation: 学习一门新语言需要循序渐进，从基础词汇开始。

vocabulary.example: Careless driving can result in serious accidents.
vocabulary.translation: 粗心驾驶可能会导致严重的事故。

vocabulary.translation: 我们需要找到一个解决环境问题的可持续方案。

sentences.chinese: 如果你讨厌蘑菇，就不要为了健康而勉强自己吃。

title: The pleasure of eating alone
paragraphs: Should you eat to live or live to eat?... a question posed by French playwright Moliere in his work ‘The Miser’. While eating is functional, and our bodies need the fuel that food provides, dining with friends or loved ones can be a wonderful experience. However, some of us often find ourselves reserving a table for one in a restaurant. But is dining alone really that bad? Maybe not.

We all have foods we like and dislike. Maybe it’s a pungent cheese or stinky fish. We sometimes hold back on things that may offend the noses of others. When dining alone, we can consume whatever we like, with the added bonus that we might be able to eat more healthily. Often, if you want a salad and your significant other wants some less healthy cuisine, you end up ordering the same. And if you don’t get the same, you might end up with food envy as you watch someone chow down on a pizza while you’re left holding the lettuce.

Have you ever spent too long debating with people which restaurant to eat in or when to meet? If dining solo, you can make the choice depending on your culinary desires at that moment and get your nourishment at exactly the time you’re hungry! And why does it have to be a restaurant? You could eat in a park, garden or even your bed – the point is, the choice is yours! That alone time also means it’s a time to switch off. According to psychologist Sherrie Bourg Carter, a bit of solitude can help your brain to unwind and may help you concentrate more.

Finally, for some, dining alone can be a necessity. For those of us who suffer from misophonia, a hatred of sound, that can in some cause PTSD, the noise of someone else masticating can be unbearable. Eating alone can save you from the extreme anxiety that may arise listening to someone smack their lips or the sloshing of saliva in their mouths! So, is eating alone bad? Well, it may not be for everyone, but there certainly are some benefits to it. Try it sometime – you might just like it!

vocabulary.entry: pose /pəʊz/ v. 提出（问题、观点等）
vocabulary.example: The philosopher posed a series of questions about human nature.
vocabulary.translation: 这位哲学家提出了一系列关于人性的问题。

vocabulary.entry: playwright /ˈpleɪraɪt/ n. 剧作家
