title: The benefits of being an introvert
paragraphs: From a young age, many of us learn the benefits of being an extrovert – those gregarious individuals who always seem to be the life and soul of the party, often outspoken and able to express their opinions easily. However, not all of us are wired that way – so is being an extrovert really better?

While thinking of extroverts, we imagine a character who is assertive, approachable, cheerful and charming. We are taught to admire these traits early on. Kids are often encouraged to interact, play and communicate with other children. It seems at times as though children are made to embrace a more outgoing lifestyle, with some people becoming pseudo-extroverts – introverts who mimic extrovert behaviour. While externally they seem to enjoy the company of others, or being in the limelight, they can still become over-extended in intense social situations.

So, while the positive aspects of being an extrovert are plain to see, what are the benefits of introversion? While extroverts thrive on social interaction, introverts are more comfortable with levels of isolation. According to Dr Berit Brogaard, a professor of philosophy, extreme solitude, such as times like the recent lockdown, does not affect introverts as much as extroverts. Lack of social contact, something extroverts thrive on, can lead to depression, loneliness, and even premature death.

But it’s not just in an extreme situation that the pros of being an introvert shine through. These people seem to have more time for contemplation and introspection and thus can become more balanced. They also tend to be good listeners and think before they speak, meaning they could become great friends. Finally, introverts are often fantastic observers, as sitting out of the focus can give you more time to watch the behaviour of others.
So, whatever your personality, either introvert or extrovert, there are clear advantages to being either, and if you meet an introvert, you might just end up with an amazing friend.

title: Minimalism vs maximalism
paragraphs: Some say you can tell a lot about a person by the way they decorate their home. We often find pleasure in the things we stick in our houses, be it trinket we bought on holiday, film memorabilium or painting to liven up walls. And when we head to others’ houses, we often see things we appreciate, but wouldn’t have in our own homes, because maybe they’re not quite to our taste. The point is, the way we decorate our homes is very personal. And while many of us have plenty of stuff, there are always people who go that little bit further. So, when it comes to minimalism and maximalism, which one appeals to you more?

Minimalism was an art movement that started in the 1950s. Its basic principles are derived from a concept of ‘less is more’ – reducing things back to their most basic. Some people took that art style and used it as a way of living. Ideas of vast open space with an organised and functional structure may spring to mind. They are usually decorated in simple pastel colour, with many minimalists opting for duotone, often just black and white. For some, especially maximalists, it may seem sparse and a bit bland to live without many things – even boring or depressing. However, living in this way is seen by many as more practical.

Maximalism is the opposite of minimalism and started in the 1970s. It embraces the core ideals that ‘more is more’. While minimalism centres around the principle of decluttering, it’s easy to imagine that a maximalist home is overflowing with items – but that’s not the base idea. It’s more about filling the space – making the most of the area. Structured excess and bold colour combined with mixed pattern is what you will see in a home like this. For a minimalist, used to more simplistic designs, it could be overwhelming. But for those who embrace it, those things give a space personality.
The way you have your home is up to you! But, if you opt for maximalism, you may need to prepare for a bit more dusting.

vocabulary.entry: functional /ˈfʌŋkʃənl/ adj. 实用的；具备功能的
vocabulary.example: The new office furniture is both functional and stylish.
vocabulary.translation: 这批新办公家具既实用又美观。

vocabulary.entry: pastel /ˈpæstl/ adj. 柔和的；淡色的
vocabulary.example: She chose a pastel blue for the bedroom walls.
vocabulary.translation: 她选了柔和的蓝色来粉刷卧室墙面。

vocabulary.entry: opt for /ɒpt fɔː/ 选择；挑选
vocabulary.example: Many people opt for organic food for health reasons.
vocabulary.translation: 出于健康考虑，很多人会选择有机食品。

vocabulary.entry: duotone /ˈdjuːətəʊn/ n. 双色；双色调
vocabulary.example: The designer used a black-and-white duotone for the poster.
vocabulary.translation: 设计师为海报采用了黑白双色的设计。

vocabulary.entry: sparse /spɑːs/ adj. 稀疏的；稀少的
vocabulary.example: Vegetation is sparse in the arid region.
vocabulary.translation: 这片干旱地区的植被十分稀少。

vocabulary.entry: bland /blænd/ adj. 平淡的；乏味的
vocabulary.example: The soup was too bland for my taste, so I added some salt.
vocabulary.translation: 这汤我喝着太淡了，就加了些盐。

vocabulary.entry: practical /ˈpræktɪkl/ adj. 实用的；切实可行的
vocabulary.example: This is a practical solution to the problem we are facing.
vocabulary.translation: 这是解决我们当前面临问题的一个切实可行的方案。

vocabulary.entry: embrace /ɪmˈbreɪs/ v. 信奉；欣然接受
vocabulary.example: The country has embraced new technologies to boost its economy.
vocabulary.translation: 这个国家已欣然采用新技术来推动经济发展。

vocabulary.entry: decluttering /dɪˈklʌtərɪŋ/ n. 清理冗余物品；整理
vocabulary.example: Decluttering can help create a more comfortable living environment.
vocabulary.translation: 清理冗余物品有助于打造更舒适的居住环境。

vocabulary.entry: overflow /ˌəʊvəˈfləʊ/ v. 充满；满得溢出
vocabulary.example: The shelves overflow with books and magazines.
vocabulary.translation: 书架上堆满了书和杂志。

vocabulary.entry: structured excess /ˈstrʌktʃəd ɪkˈses/ 规整的繁复感
vocabulary.example: The room's design features structured excess rather than messy piles of items.
vocabulary.translation: 这个房间的设计特点是规整的繁复感，而非杂乱堆积的物品。

vocabulary.entry: bold /bəʊld/ adj. 大胆的；醒目的
vocabulary.example: The advertisement uses bold colours to attract attention.
vocabulary.translation: 这则广告用醒目的色彩来吸引注意力。

vocabulary.entry: mixed pattern /mɪkst ˈpætn/ 混搭图案
vocabulary.example: The sofa is covered with fabric featuring a mixed pattern of stripes and flowers.
vocabulary.translation: 这张沙发的面料是条纹与花卉的混搭图案。

vocabulary.entry: overwhelming /ˌəʊvəˈwelmɪŋ/ adj. 令人不知所措的；眼花缭乱的
vocabulary.example: The amount of information available online can be overwhelming.
vocabulary.translation: 网上海量的信息会让人不知所措。

vocabulary.entry: personality /ˌpɜːsəˈnæləti/ n. 个性；特色
vocabulary.example: The unique decorations give the café a lot of personality.
vocabulary.translation: 这些独特的装饰赋予了这家咖啡馆十足的特色。

sentences.english: Some say you can tell a lot about a person by the way they decorate their home.
sentences.chinese: 有人说，从一个人装饰家的方式就能看出他的很多特质。

sentences.english: We often find pleasure in the things we stick in our houses, be it trinket we bought on holiday, film memorabilium or painting to liven up walls.
sentences.chinese: 我们总乐于在家中摆放一些物件，比如度假时买的小饰品、电影纪念品，或是能让墙面焕发生机的画作。

sentences.english: And when we head to others’ houses, we often see things we appreciate, but wouldn’t have in our own homes, because maybe they’re not quite to our taste.
sentences.chinese: 当我们去别人家做客时，也常会看到一些自己欣赏、却不会放在自家的东西，可能只是因为这些东西不太合自己的口味。

sentences.english: The point is, the way we decorate our homes is very personal.
sentences.chinese: 关键是，家装的方式极具个人色彩。

sentences.english: And while many of us have plenty of stuff, there are always people who go that little bit further.
sentences.chinese: 虽然我们很多人家里的东西已经不少，但总有人会想要更多。

sentences.english: So, when it comes to minimalism and maximalism, which one appeals to you more?
sentences.chinese: 那么，说到极简主义和极繁主义这两种风格，你更偏爱哪一种呢？

sentences.english: Minimalism was an art movement that started in the 1950s. Its basic principles are derived from a concept of ‘less is more’ – reducing things back to their most basic.
sentences.chinese: 极简主义是20世纪50年代兴起的一场艺术运动，其基本原则源于“少即是多”的理念——将事物还原至最本质的状态。

sentences.english: Some people took that art style and used it as a way of living.
sentences.chinese: 一些人将这种艺术风格运用到了生活方式中。

sentences.english: Ideas of vast open space with an organised and functional structure may spring to mind.
sentences.chinese: 人们想到这种风格，往往会浮现出开阔敞亮、布局规整且实用性强的空间画面。

sentences.english: They are usually decorated in simple pastel colour, with many minimalists opting for duotone, often just black and white.
sentences.chinese: 这类家居通常采用简约的柔和色调，许多极简主义者还会选择双色搭配，通常就是黑与白。

sentences.english: For some, especially maximalists, it may seem sparse and a bit bland to live without many things – even boring or depressing.
sentences.chinese: 对有些人来说，尤其是极繁主义者，生活中少了很多物件，会显得空旷单调，甚至有些乏味沉闷。

sentences.english: However, living in this way is seen by many as more practical.
sentences.chinese: 但在很多人看来，这种生活方式其实更为实用。

sentences.english: Maximalism is the opposite of minimalism and started in the 1970s. It embraces the core ideals that ‘more is more’.
sentences.chinese: 极繁主义诞生于20世纪70年代，是极简主义的对立面，它信奉“多即是多”的核心理念。

sentences.english: While minimalism centres around the principle of decluttering, it’s easy to imagine that a maximalist home is overflowing with items – but that’s not the base idea.
sentences.chinese: 极简主义的核心是清理冗余物品，由此很容易让人联想到极繁主义的家会堆满各种物件——但这并非其本意。

sentences.english: It’s more about filling the space – making the most of the area.
sentences.chinese: 极繁主义更强调充实空间，充分利用每一处区域。

sentences.english: Structured excess and bold colour combined with mixed pattern is what you will see in a home like this.
sentences.chinese: 这种风格的家居，呈现出的是规整的繁复感、大胆的色彩运用以及多样的图案混搭。

sentences.english: For a minimalist, used to more simplistic designs, it could be overwhelming.
sentences.chinese: 对于习惯了简约设计的极简主义者而言，这样的空间可能会让人觉得眼花缭乱。

sentences.english: But for those who embrace it, those things give a space personality.
sentences.chinese: 但对钟爱极繁风格的人来说，这些元素恰恰赋予了空间独特的个性。

sentences.english: The way you have your home is up to you!
sentences.chinese: 家的风格终究由你做主！

sentences.english: But, if you opt for maximalism, you may need to prepare for a bit more dusting.
sentences.chinese: 不过，如果你选择了极繁主义，那可得做好多花些时间打扫除尘的准备。

title: How to be a better saver
paragraphs: We often try to save money for a variety of different reasons. It might be to save up for a new computer, put money aside into a rainy-day fund or put a deposit down for a mortgage on a house. Learning how to save is important, but a recent study showed that over half of all 22 – 29-year-olds living in the UK have no savings at all. Did they splurge and splash out on too many things, or are there other factors? And how can we become better savers?

Many young people in the UK choose to live away from home, and the cost of renting can impact the amount we can tuck away in our savings. On top of that, according to a 2017 study, there is a huge pay gap in people in their twenties in the UK, with the top 10% earning 4.3 times per week as the lowest earners. Possibly the mentality of ‘saving more when I earn more’ has crept in. However, there were some positives, with the number of people in debt, not including student loans for university, having fallen from 49% 10 years ago to 37%.

So, how can we improve our ability to save? First off, put a stop to those impulse buys. Ask yourself if you really need to buy something, even if it is on sale or looks like a bargain. One way you could control your spending urges is by using cash rather than card. Withdrawing cash before you go to a restaurant or shopping sets a fixed budget you must adhere to. Also, any change that comes from your transactions when you’re using cash can be put in jar and deposited into your account. Finally, setting up a standing order from your current account into your savings just after you receive your salary will ensure you have some money set aside for a time that you might need it. Just after getting paid is a good idea for this as it means you save before you’ve had the chance to spend.

While there is some good news about debt for the twenty-somethings in the UK, the fact that over half have no savings is seen as a cause for concern. While it could be due to some economic disparity, there may be some other factors at play. However, there are some actions we can take to help us all become better savers.

vocabulary.entry: rainy-day fund /ˈreɪni deɪ fʌnd/ n. 应急基金
vocabulary.example: It's wise to build a rainy-day fund for unexpected expenses.
vocabulary.translation: 为意外开支设立应急基金是明智之举。

vocabulary.entry: deposit /dɪˈpɒzɪt/ n. （购房等的）定金，首付
vocabulary.example: She saved hard to pay a deposit on a flat.
vocabulary.translation: 她努力攒钱，为买公寓支付了首付。

vocabulary.entry: mortgage /ˈmɔːɡɪdʒ/ n. 按揭贷款
vocabulary.example: He took out a mortgage to buy his first house.
vocabulary.translation: 他办理了按揭贷款，买下了自己的第一套房。

vocabulary.entry: splurge /splɜːdʒ/ v. 挥霍，乱花钱
vocabulary.example: She likes to splurge on luxury skincare products occasionally.
vocabulary.translation: 她偶尔会挥霍一把，买些奢华的护肤品。

vocabulary.entry: splash out /splæʃ aʊt/ 挥霍金钱，大手大脚地花钱
vocabulary.example: They decided to splash out on a fancy meal for their anniversary.
vocabulary.translation: 他们决定挥霍一次，为纪念日吃一顿大餐。

vocabulary.entry: tuck away /tʌk əˈweɪ/ 储存，存（钱）
vocabulary.example: He tries to tuck away a small amount of money every month.
vocabulary.translation: 他每月都会试着存一小笔钱。

vocabulary.entry: pay gap /peɪ ɡæp/ n. 收入差距
vocabulary.example: The report highlights the pay gap between men and women in the industry.
vocabulary.translation: 这份报告强调了该行业男女之间的收入差距。

vocabulary.entry: mentality /menˈtæləti/ n. 心态，思维方式
vocabulary.example: He has a positive mentality towards challenges in work.
vocabulary.translation: 他对工作中的挑战抱有积极的心态。

vocabulary.entry: creep in /kriːp ɪn/ 悄然出现，渐渐产生
vocabulary.example: Doubts began to creep in as the deadline approached.
vocabulary.translation: 随着截止日期的临近，疑虑开始悄然浮现。

vocabulary.entry: disparity /dɪˈspærəti/ n. 差距，差异
vocabulary.example: There is a huge disparity in living standards between the two regions.
vocabulary.translation: 这两个地区的生活水平存在巨大差异。

vocabulary.entry: impulse buy /ˈɪmpʌls baɪ/ n. 冲动消费，即兴购买的物品
vocabulary.example: That dress was an impulse buy; I never wear it now.
vocabulary.translation: 那条裙子是我一时冲动买的，现在根本不穿。

vocabulary.entry: bargain /ˈbɑːɡən/ n. 特价商品，便宜货
vocabulary.example: She picked up a few bargains in the summer sale.
vocabulary.translation: 她在夏季大甩卖中淘到了几件便宜货。

vocabulary.entry: urge /ɜːdʒ/ n. 强烈的欲望，冲动
vocabulary.example: He felt a sudden urge to eat something sweet.
vocabulary.translation: 他突然很想吃点甜食。

vocabulary.entry: adhere to /ədˈhɪə tuː/ 遵守，坚持（规定、承诺等）
vocabulary.example: All members must adhere to the club's rules and regulations.
vocabulary.translation: 所有会员都必须遵守俱乐部的规章制度。

vocabulary.entry: transaction /trænˈzækʃn/ n. 交易，业务往来
vocabulary.example: The bank charges a fee for each online transaction.
vocabulary.translation: 这家银行对每笔网上交易都收取手续费。

vocabulary.entry: standing order /ˈstændɪŋ ɔːdə/ n. （银行的）定期自动转账指令
vocabulary.example: I set up a standing order to pay the rent every month.
vocabulary.translation: 我设置了定期自动转账，每月支付房租。

vocabulary.entry: current account /ˈkʌrənt əˈkaʊnt/ n. 活期存款账户
vocabulary.example: I need to transfer money from my savings account to my current account.
vocabulary.translation: 我需要把钱从储蓄账户转到活期账户。

vocabulary.entry: savings account /ˈseɪvɪŋz əˈkaʊnt/ n. 储蓄账户
vocabulary.example: The savings account offers a higher interest rate than the current one.
vocabulary.translation: 储蓄账户的利率比活期账户高。

vocabulary.entry: set aside /set əˈsaɪd/ 留出，拨出（时间、金钱等）
vocabulary.example: She sets aside an hour every day for reading.
vocabulary.translation: 她每天都留出一小时的时间看书。

vocabulary.entry: cause for concern /kɔːz fɔː kənˈsɜːn/ 令人担忧的原因
vocabulary.example: The rising crime rate is a major cause for concern in the city.
vocabulary.translation: 不断上升的犯罪率是这座城市一个主要的担忧点。

vocabulary.entry: at play /æt pleɪ/ 起作用，参与其中
vocabulary.example: Several factors are at play in the success of this project.
vocabulary.translation: 有几个因素共同促成了这个项目的成功。

vocabulary.entry: on sale /ɒn seɪl/ 特价出售，降价促销
vocabulary.example: Most of the winter clothing is on sale in the store now.
vocabulary.translation: 这家店现在大部分冬装都在打折。

vocabulary.entry: fixed budget /fɪkst ˈbʌdʒɪt/ n. 固定预算
vocabulary.example: We have to work within a fixed budget for the event.
vocabulary.translation: 我们必须在固定的预算内筹备这场活动。

vocabulary.entry: rent /rent/ n. 租金
vocabulary.example: The rent for this apartment includes water and electricity bills.
vocabulary.translation: 这套公寓的租金包含水电费。

vocabulary.entry: debt /det/ n. 债务，欠款
vocabulary.example: He is trying his best to pay off his debts as soon as possible.
vocabulary.translation: 他正努力尽快还清所有欠款。

sentences.english: We often try to save money for a variety of different reasons.
sentences.chinese: 我们总会出于各种各样的原因存钱。

sentences.english: It might be to save up for a new computer, put money aside into a rainy-day fund or put a deposit down for a mortgage on a house.
sentences.chinese: 可能是为了攒钱买一台新电脑，为应急基金预留一笔钱，或是为买房的按揭贷款支付首付。

sentences.english: Learning how to save is important, but a recent study showed that over half of all 22 – 29-year-olds living in the UK have no savings at all.
sentences.chinese: 学会存钱至关重要，但最近一项研究显示，在英国22至29岁的人群中，超过半数的人根本没有存款。

sentences.english: Did they splurge and splash out on too many things, or are there other factors?
sentences.chinese: 是他们挥霍无度、花钱大手大脚，还是另有原因？

sentences.english: And how can we become better savers?
sentences.chinese: 我们又该如何成为更会存钱的人呢？

sentences.english: Many young people in the UK choose to live away from home, and the cost of renting can impact the amount we can tuck away in our savings.
sentences.chinese: 许多英国年轻人选择离家独居，高昂的房租会直接影响我们能存下的钱数。

sentences.english: On top of that, according to a 2017 study, there is a huge pay gap in people in their twenties in the UK, with the top 10% earning 4.3 times per week as the lowest earners.
sentences.chinese: 此外，2017年的一项研究表明，英国二十多岁年轻人的收入差距悬殊，收入最高的10%人群周薪是收入最低人群的4.3倍。

sentences.english: Possibly the mentality of ‘saving more when I earn more’ has crept in.
sentences.chinese: 或许正是“等赚得多了再多存钱”的心态在悄然作祟。

sentences.english: However, there were some positives, with the number of people in debt, not including student loans for university, having fallen from 49% 10 years ago to 37%.
sentences.chinese: 不过也有一些积极的趋势：不含大学助学贷款在内的负债人群比例，已从十年前的49%降至如今的37%。

sentences.english: So, how can we improve our ability to save?
sentences.chinese: 那么，我们该如何提升存钱能力呢？

sentences.english: First off, put a stop to those impulse buys.
sentences.chinese: 首先，杜绝冲动消费。

sentences.english: Ask yourself if you really need to buy something, even if it is on sale or looks like a bargain.
sentences.chinese: 就算商品正在打折，或是看起来很划算，也要先问问自己是否真的需要。

sentences.english: One way you could control your spending urges is by using cash rather than card.
sentences.chinese: 控制消费欲望的一个办法是使用现金而非银行卡支付。

sentences.english: Withdrawing cash before you go to a restaurant or shopping sets a fixed budget you must adhere to.
sentences.chinese: 去餐厅吃饭或购物前先取好现金，这样就能设定一个必须遵守的固定预算。

sentences.english: Also, any change that comes from your transactions when you’re using cash can be put in jar and deposited into your account.
sentences.chinese: 此外，用现金交易时收到的零钱可以放进存钱罐，之后再存入银行账户。

sentences.english: Finally, setting up a standing order from your current account into your savings just after you receive your salary will ensure you have some money set aside for a time that you might need it.
sentences.chinese: 最后，在发薪后立即设置自动转账，把钱从活期账户转入储蓄账户，这样就能确保为不时之需存下一笔钱。

sentences.english: Just after getting paid is a good idea for this as it means you save before you’ve had the chance to spend.
sentences.chinese: 发薪之后马上就转是一个好主意，因为这意味着你还没有花钱的机会，钱就已经被存起来了。

sentences.english: While there is some good news about debt for the twenty-somethings in the UK, the fact that over half have no savings is seen as a cause for concern.
sentences.chinese: 尽管英国二十多岁人群的负债情况有了些许好转，但半数以上的人毫无存款这一事实，依然引发了人们的担忧。

sentences.english: While it could be due to some economic disparity, there may be some other factors at play.
sentences.chinese: 这或许是经济差距造成的，但也可能涉及其他因素。

sentences.english: However, there are some actions we can take to help us all become better savers.
sentences.chinese: 不过，我们确实可以采取一些措施，让自己变得更擅长储蓄。

title: AI in the home
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence becoming self-aware and exterminating the human race is a common theme in science fiction. But the levels of high intelligence that AI could reach is a real concern among some scientists. But with more talk of AI and smart devices in the home, what are the positives of bringing these things into your life?

Hans Rosling, a professor of international health, once spoke about the impact and changes that the washing machine made. The once arduous task of cleaning clothes by hand was taken on by a machine and freed up more time for other activities. There are so many smart devices that you can fill your home with. Imagine waking up to find a piping hot, freshly brewed cup of coffee, spotless floors that have been recently vacuumed and the house set to the perfect temperature. With smart devices, these things can happen while you sleep. The potential to pre-program and automate parts of your life means that you can focus on other tasks in your life.

But there is a difference between smart devices and AI. Smart devices are the things that get on with the tasks, while AI can ‘think’ or interact, and can be used to control the smart devices. There are many voice-activated AI systems which can control the smart devices around your home. You can ask these devices to start making coffee, dim the lights when they’re too bright or even make sure the house is secure. You can inquire as to the weather outside, ask them to blare out music or search the internet for you when you have a burning question about history or the latest cooking recipes. Some of these devices even have a sense of humour, and upon asking them certain questions, they will retort. In short, in some ways, they can act as company.

But how far will it go? Well, we already have self-driving cars and sentient tech that can automatically order the delivery of certain products to restock our fridge when we’re running low, but often in films and games we see humanoid robots taking over all of the domestic duties. It seems for now, that those things only live in our imaginations, but we could be seeing them sooner than we think.

vocabulary.entry: self-aware /ˌself əˈweə(r)/ adj. 拥有自我意识的
vocabulary.example: The concept of a self-aware machine remains a topic of debate among tech experts.
vocabulary.translation: 拥有自我意识的机器这一概念，至今仍是科技专家们争论的话题。

vocabulary.entry: exterminate /ɪkˈstɜːmɪneɪt/ v. 灭绝；根除
vocabulary.example: Efforts are being made to exterminate the invasive species in this region.
vocabulary.translation: 人们正采取行动，根除该地区的入侵物种。

vocabulary.entry: arduous /ˈɑːdjuəs/ adj. 艰巨的；繁重的
vocabulary.example: The team faced an arduous journey through the mountainous terrain.
vocabulary.translation: 这支队伍要踏上一段穿越山区的艰苦旅程。

vocabulary.entry: brew /bruː/ v. 冲泡（茶、咖啡等）；酿造
vocabulary.example: She prefers to brew her own coffee rather than buy instant coffee.
vocabulary.translation: 她更喜欢自己煮咖啡，而不是买速溶咖啡。

vocabulary.entry: vacuum /ˈvækjuːm/ v. 用吸尘器清扫
vocabulary.example: I usually vacuum the living room every Saturday morning.
vocabulary.translation: 我通常每周六早上用吸尘器打扫客厅。

vocabulary.entry: pre-program /ˌpriː ˈprəʊɡræm/ v. 预先设定程序
vocabulary.example: You can pre-program the smart oven to start cooking at a specific time.
vocabulary.translation: 你可以给智能烤箱预先设定程序，让它在指定时间开始烹饪。

vocabulary.entry: automate /ˈɔːtəmeɪt/ v. 使自动化
vocabulary.example: The factory plans to automate more production lines next year.
vocabulary.translation: 这家工厂计划明年让更多生产线实现自动化。

vocabulary.entry: voice-activated /ˌvɔɪs ˈæktɪveɪtɪd/ adj. 声控的
vocabulary.example: This voice-activated assistant can help you manage your daily schedule.
vocabulary.translation: 这款声控助手可以帮你管理日常日程。

vocabulary.entry: dim /dɪm/ v. 调暗（灯光）；使暗淡
vocabulary.example: He dimmed the lights to create a more romantic atmosphere.
vocabulary.translation: 他调暗了灯光，营造出更浪漫的氛围。

vocabulary.entry: inquire /ɪnˈkwaɪə(r)/ v. 询问；打听
vocabulary.example: She called the hotel to inquire about the availability of rooms.
vocabulary.translation: 她打电话给酒店，询问房间的空余情况。

vocabulary.entry: blare /bleə(r)/ v. 高声播放；发出刺耳的声音
vocabulary.example: The radio was blaring music so loud that we couldn't hear each other talk.
vocabulary.translation: 收音机高声播放着音乐，吵得我们都听不清彼此说话。

vocabulary.entry: burning /ˈbɜːnɪŋ/ adj. 迫切的；热切的
vocabulary.example: She had a burning desire to find out the truth behind the incident.
vocabulary.translation: 她迫切想要查明这起事件背后的真相。

vocabulary.entry: retort /rɪˈtɔːt/ v. 反驳；回嘴（愤怒或风趣地）
vocabulary.example: When criticized for being late, she retorted that the bus had broken down.
vocabulary.translation: 当被指责迟到时，她反驳说公交车抛锚了。

vocabulary.entry: sentient /ˈsentiənt/ adj. 有感知能力的；有感觉的
vocabulary.example: The novel describes a world where sentient robots coexist with humans.
vocabulary.translation: 这部小说描绘了一个有感知能力的机器人与人类共存的世界。

vocabulary.entry: restock /ˌriːˈstɒk/ v. 补充存货；重新进货
vocabulary.example: The supermarket needs to restock the shelves with fresh vegetables every morning.
vocabulary.translation: 这家超市每天早上都要给货架补充新鲜蔬菜。

vocabulary.entry: humanoid /ˈhjuːmənɔɪd/ adj. 人形的；类人的
vocabulary.example: The lab has developed a humanoid robot that can mimic human facial expressions.
vocabulary.translation: 该实验室研发出一款能模仿人类面部表情的人形机器人。

vocabulary.entry: domestic /dəˈmestɪk/ adj. 家务的；家庭的
vocabulary.example: She spends a lot of time on domestic chores like cleaning and cooking.
vocabulary.translation: 她花很多时间在打扫、做饭这类家务上。

vocabulary.entry: theme /θiːm/ n. 主题；主旋律
vocabulary.example: The theme of environmental protection runs through the whole film.
vocabulary.translation: 环保主题贯穿了整部电影。

vocabulary.entry: concern /kənˈsɜːn/ n. 担忧；关切的事
vocabulary.example: The safety of the new product is a major concern for consumers.
vocabulary.translation: 这款新产品的安全性是消费者关注的重点。

vocabulary.entry: potential /pəˈtenʃl/ n. 潜力；可能性
vocabulary.example: The young musician has great potential to become a star.
vocabulary.translation: 这位年轻的音乐家有很大的潜力成为明星。

vocabulary.entry: interact /ˌɪntərˈækt/ v. 互动；交流
vocabulary.example: Teachers should encourage students to interact with each other in class.
vocabulary.translation: 教师应鼓励学生在课堂上相互交流。

vocabulary.entry: secure /sɪˈkjʊə(r)/ adj. 安全的；可靠的
vocabulary.example: We need to take measures to keep our personal information secure online.
vocabulary.translation: 我们需要采取措施，确保个人信息在网上的安全。

vocabulary.entry: recipe /ˈresəpi/ n. 食谱；烹饪方法
vocabulary.example: She found a delicious cake recipe in a magazine.
vocabulary.translation: 她在一本杂志上找到了一份美味的蛋糕食谱。

vocabulary.entry: company /ˈkʌmpəni/ n. 陪伴；做伴
vocabulary.example: Dogs are known as man's best friend because they provide loyal company.
vocabulary.translation: 狗被称为人类最好的朋友，因为它们能给予忠诚的陪伴。

vocabulary.entry: terrain /təˈreɪn/ n. 地形；地势
vocabulary.example: The army trained hard to adapt to the harsh desert terrain.
vocabulary.translation: 这支军队刻苦训练，以适应恶劣的沙漠地形。

sentences.english: Artificial intelligence becoming self-aware and exterminating the human race is a common theme in science fiction.
sentences.chinese: 人工智能拥有自我意识并灭绝人类，是科幻作品中常见的主题。

sentences.english: But the levels of high intelligence that AI could reach is a real concern among some scientists.
sentences.chinese: 但人工智能可能达到的高智能水平，确实引发了一些科学家的担忧。

sentences.english: But with more talk of AI and smart devices in the home, what are the positives of bringing these things into your life?
sentences.chinese: 不过，随着人们对人工智能和家用智能设备的讨论越来越多，将这些事物引入生活又有哪些好处呢？

sentences.english: Hans Rosling, a professor of international health, once spoke about the impact and changes that the washing machine made.
sentences.chinese: 国际卫生学教授汉斯·罗斯林曾谈及洗衣机带来的影响与变革。

sentences.english: The once arduous task of cleaning clothes by hand was taken on by a machine and freed up more time for other activities.
sentences.chinese: 曾经繁重的手工洗衣劳动被机器接手，人们得以腾出更多时间投入其他活动。

sentences.english: There are so many smart devices that you can fill your home with.
sentences.chinese: 如今，有各种各样的智能设备可以进驻家庭。

sentences.english: Imagine waking up to find a piping hot, freshly brewed cup of coffee, spotless floors that have been recently vacuumed and the house set to the perfect temperature.
sentences.chinese: 试想一下，你一觉醒来，就有一杯刚煮好的滚烫咖啡，地板被打扫得一尘不染，室温也调节得恰到好处。

sentences.english: With smart devices, these things can happen while you sleep.
sentences.chinese: 有了智能设备，这些事情在你熟睡时就能完成。

sentences.english: The potential to pre-program and automate parts of your life means that you can focus on other tasks in your life.
sentences.chinese: 预先设定程序、将生活中的部分事务自动化，这种可能性意味着你可以把精力集中在生活中的其他事情上。

sentences.english: But there is a difference between smart devices and AI.
sentences.chinese: 但智能设备和人工智能之间存在区别。

sentences.english: Smart devices are the things that get on with the tasks, while AI can ‘think’ or interact, and can be used to control the smart devices.
sentences.chinese: 智能设备是执行具体任务的工具，而人工智能能够“思考”或与人互动，还可以用来控制智能设备。

sentences.english: There are many voice-activated AI systems which can control the smart devices around your home.
sentences.chinese: 市面上有许多声控人工智能系统，能够操控家中的各类智能设备。

sentences.english: You can ask these devices to start making coffee, dim the lights when they’re too bright or even make sure the house is secure.
sentences.chinese: 你可以吩咐它们煮咖啡、在灯光太亮时调暗亮度，甚至让它们确保家居安全。

sentences.english: You can inquire as to the weather outside, ask them to blare out music or search the internet for you when you have a burning question about history or the latest cooking recipes.
sentences.chinese: 你可以询问室外天气，让它们播放音乐，或是在你对某个历史问题充满好奇、想找最新食谱时，让它们帮你搜索互联网。

sentences.english: Some of these devices even have a sense of humour, and upon asking them certain questions, they will retort.
sentences.chinese: 有些这类设备甚至还带有幽默感，当你向它们提出特定问题时，它们会给出俏皮的回应。

sentences.english: In short, in some ways, they can act as company.
sentences.chinese: 简而言之，在某种程度上，它们可以充当陪伴者的角色。

sentences.english: But how far will it go?
sentences.chinese: 但人工智能的发展会走向何方呢？

sentences.english: Well, we already have self-driving cars and sentient tech that can automatically order the delivery of certain products to restock our fridge when we’re running low, but often in films and games we see humanoid robots taking over all of the domestic duties.
sentences.chinese: 目前，我们已经拥有了自动驾驶汽车，还有具备感知能力的技术——当冰箱里的食材不足时，它能自动下单订购相关商品进行补货。不过在电影和游戏中，我们经常看到人形机器人包揽所有家务的场景。

sentences.english: It seems for now, that those things only live in our imaginations, but we could be seeing them sooner than we think.
sentences.chinese: 眼下，这些景象似乎还只存在于想象之中，但说不定我们离见到它们的日子，比预想的要早得多。

title: Getting ready for university
paragraphs: You’ve studied hard, you’ve got the grades and now you’re off to university! This is the journey that many students are taking, but how prepared are they to leave home, stand on their own two feet and be self-sufficient? One study, carried out by the Higher Education Policy Institute and Unite Students in 2017, suggested that as well as being excited and nervous, many students are deeply ill-informed about what to expect.

Of course, flying the nest to go to university is the opportunity of a lifetime, but to make the most of it needs some preparation before you arrive. This means learning life skills such as cooking and cleaning. You’ll no longer be able to rely on Mum and Dad to feed you or clear up after you, so try to learn how to make some staple dishes that are quick and easy to prepare. Graduate Peter Rogers told the BBC: “I didn’t really have anything other than rudimentary cookery skills before I went to university and found learning to cook was reasonably enjoyable.” Other things to do while at home is to practise some of those household chores, like operating the washing machine or ironing your clothes!

These domestic skills will come in useful because students will probably be living with others such as in a flat share or shared campus-based accommodation. This will also require taking responsibility for managing their finances because, apart from tuition fees, accommodation is likely to be the biggest cost for students living away from home. However, the Higher Education Policy Institute and Unite Students study found only about half of the would-be students surveyed identified rent as the biggest expense and concluded that this suggests more should be done to help in the transition between school and university.

New students are going to have to be sociable as well – not just relying on old friends at home. Going to university requires meeting new people and making new friends. This often begins in Freshers’ Week although journalism student Emmeke Megannety warns that: “People starting uni need to remember that the people you meet in your first week will not necessarily be your friends for life.” But whatever your expectations, it’s good to be prepared for the time of your life.

vocabulary.entry: self-sufficient /ˌself səˈfɪʃnt/ adj. 自给自足的；能独立生活的
vocabulary.example: After a few months of living alone, she became more self-sufficient.
vocabulary.translation: 独自生活几个月后，她变得更加能自给自足了。

vocabulary.entry: ill-informed /ˌɪl ɪnˈfɔːmd/ adj. 所知甚少的；消息不灵通的
vocabulary.example: He made an ill-informed decision based on incomplete data.
vocabulary.translation: 他基于不完整的数据做出了一个考虑不周的决定。

vocabulary.entry: fly the nest /flaɪ ðə nest/ 离家独立生活
vocabulary.example: Many young people fly the nest when they go to college.
vocabulary.translation: 许多年轻人上大学时就离家独立生活了。

vocabulary.term: stand on one's own two feet
vocabulary.entry: stand on one's own two feet /stænd ɒn wʌnz əʊn tuː fiːt/ 独立自主
vocabulary.example: It's time for you to stand on your own two feet and make your own decisions.
vocabulary.translation: 你该学会独立自主，自己做决定了。

vocabulary.entry: opportunity of a lifetime /ˌɒpəˈtjuːnəti ɒv ˈlaɪftaɪm/ 一生难得的机遇
vocabulary.example: Winning the scholarship was an opportunity of a lifetime for her.
vocabulary.translation: 赢得这份奖学金对她来说是一生难得的机遇。

vocabulary.entry: make the most of /meɪk ðə məʊst ɒv/ 充分利用
vocabulary.example: You should make the most of the chance to study abroad.
vocabulary.translation: 你应该充分利用这次出国留学的机会。

vocabulary.entry: staple dish /ˈsteɪpl dɪʃ/ n. 家常菜；主食菜肴
vocabulary.example: Rice and stir-fried vegetables are staple dishes in many Asian households.
vocabulary.translation: 米饭和炒蔬菜是许多亚洲家庭的家常菜。

vocabulary.entry: rudimentary /ˌruːdɪˈmentri/ adj. 基础的；初步的
vocabulary.example: The course provides only rudimentary introduction to the subject.
vocabulary.translation: 这门课程只对该学科做了基础的介绍。

vocabulary.entry: cookery /ˈkʊkəri/ n. 烹饪术；烹饪
vocabulary.example: She attended a cookery class to learn how to bake bread.
vocabulary.translation: 她参加了一个烹饪班，学习如何烤面包。

vocabulary.entry: household chore /ˈhaʊshəʊld tʃɔː(r)/ n. 家务琐事
vocabulary.example: Washing dishes is one of the most common household chores.
vocabulary.translation: 洗碗是最常见的家务琐事之一。

vocabulary.entry: iron /ˈaɪən/ v. 熨烫（衣物）
vocabulary.example: She spent the afternoon ironing all her shirts.
vocabulary.translation: 她花了一个下午熨烫所有的衬衫。

vocabulary.entry: accommodation /əˌkɒməˈdeɪʃn/ n. 住处；住宿
vocabulary.example: The university provides cheap accommodation for first-year students.
vocabulary.translation: 这所大学为大一新生提供廉价的住宿。

vocabulary.entry: tuition fee /tjuˈɪʃn fiː/ n. 学费
vocabulary.example: Many students take out loans to pay their tuition fees.
vocabulary.translation: 许多学生贷款来支付学费。

vocabulary.entry: finance /ˈfaɪnæns/ n. 财务状况；资金
vocabulary.example: He needs to improve his management of personal finance.
vocabulary.translation: 他需要改进对个人财务的管理。

vocabulary.entry: expense /ɪkˈspens/ n. 开销；花费
vocabulary.example: Accommodation is our biggest expense when travelling abroad.
vocabulary.translation: 出国旅行时，住宿费是我们最大的开销。

vocabulary.entry: would-be /ˈwʊd bi/ adj. 未来的；准的
vocabulary.example: The book offers advice to would-be entrepreneurs.
vocabulary.translation: 这本书为准创业者提供了建议。

vocabulary.entry: identify /aɪˈdentɪfaɪ/ v. 确认；认出
vocabulary.example: She was asked to identify the suspect from a lineup of photos.
vocabulary.translation: 她被要求从一排照片中辨认出嫌疑人。

vocabulary.entry: transition /trænˈzɪʃn/ n. 过渡；转变
vocabulary.example: The transition from school to work can be difficult for young people.
vocabulary.translation: 从学校到职场的转变对年轻人来说可能很难。

vocabulary.entry: sociable /ˈsəʊʃəbl/ adj. 好交际的；合群的
vocabulary.example: She is a sociable person who enjoys meeting new people.
vocabulary.translation: 她是个爱交际的人，喜欢结识新朋友。

vocabulary.entry: Freshers’ Week /ˈfreʃəz wiːk/ n. 新生周
vocabulary.example: Freshers’ Week is a great time to make new friends at university.
vocabulary.translation: 新生周是在大学里结交新朋友的好时机。

vocabulary.entry: flat share /flæt ʃeə(r)/ n. 合租公寓
vocabulary.example: He lives in a flat share with three other students.
vocabulary.translation: 他和另外三名学生合租一套公寓。

vocabulary.entry: campus-based /ˈkæmpəs beɪst/ adj. 基于校园的
vocabulary.example: The university offers campus-based accommodation for students.
vocabulary.translation: 这所大学为学生提供校内住宿。

vocabulary.entry: responsibility /rɪˌspɒnsəˈbɪləti/ n. 责任；职责
vocabulary.example: Taking care of your own health is your personal responsibility.
vocabulary.translation: 照顾好自己的健康是你个人的责任。

vocabulary.entry: rely on /rɪˈlaɪ ɒn/ 依赖；依靠
vocabulary.example: You can't always rely on your parents to solve your problems.
vocabulary.translation: 你不能总是依赖父母来解决你的问题。

vocabulary.entry: journalism /ˈdʒɜːnəlɪzəm/ n. 新闻业；新闻学
vocabulary.example: She studied journalism at university and now works for a newspaper.
vocabulary.translation: 她大学时学的是新闻学，现在在一家报社工作。

sentences.english: You’ve studied hard, you’ve got the grades and now you’re off to university!
sentences.chinese: 你努力学习，拿到了满意的成绩，如今即将踏入大学校园！

sentences.english: This is the journey that many students are taking, but how prepared are they to leave home, stand on their own two feet and be self-sufficient?
sentences.chinese: 这是许多学生都会踏上的旅程，但他们是否做好了离家的准备，能否真正独立生活、自给自足呢？

sentences.english: One study, carried out by the Higher Education Policy Institute and Unite Students in 2017, suggested that as well as being excited and nervous, many students are deeply ill-informed about what to expect.
sentences.chinese: 高等教育政策研究所与联合学生公寓在2017年开展的一项研究表明，许多学生在满怀期待与忐忑的同时，对于大学生活的实际情况也知之甚少。

sentences.english: Of course, flying the nest to go to university is the opportunity of a lifetime, but to make the most of it needs some preparation before you arrive.
sentences.chinese: 当然，离家上大学是一生难得的机遇，但要想充分利用这段时光，就需要在入学前做好一些准备。

sentences.english: This means learning life skills such as cooking and cleaning.
sentences.chinese: 这意味着要学习烹饪、打扫这类生活技能。

sentences.english: You’ll no longer be able to rely on Mum and Dad to feed you or clear up after you, so try to learn how to make some staple dishes that are quick and easy to prepare.
sentences.chinese: 你不能再依赖父母为你做饭、收拾残局了，所以不妨学着做几道简单快捷易上手的家常菜。

sentences.english: Graduate Peter Rogers told the BBC: “I didn’t really have anything other than rudimentary cookery skills before I went to university and found learning to cook was reasonably enjoyable.”
sentences.chinese: 毕业生彼得·罗杰斯在接受BBC采访时表示：“上大学前，我只掌握了一些最基础的烹饪技能，后来发现学着做饭其实还挺有意思的。”

sentences.english: Other things to do while at home is to practise some of those household chores, like operating the washing machine or ironing your clothes!
sentences.chinese: 在家时还可以练习一些家务，比如操作洗衣机、熨烫衣物等等！

sentences.english: These domestic skills will come in useful because students will probably be living with others such as in a flat share or shared campus-based accommodation.
sentences.chinese: 这些居家技能迟早会派上用场，因为学生很可能会和别人合租公寓，或是住进校内的集体宿舍。

sentences.english: This will also require taking responsibility for managing their finances because, apart from tuition fees, accommodation is likely to be the biggest cost for students living away from home.
sentences.chinese: 这也意味着学生需要承担起管理个人财务的责任，因为对于离家在外的学生来说，除了学费，住宿费很可能就是最大的开销。

sentences.english: However, the Higher Education Policy Institute and Unite Students study found only about half of the would-be students surveyed identified rent as the biggest expense and concluded that this suggests more should be done to help in the transition between school and university.
sentences.chinese: 但高等教育政策研究所与联合学生公寓的这项研究发现，在受访的准大学生中，只有约半数人认为房租是最大的支出。研究结论指出，这意味着需要采取更多措施，帮助学生顺利完成从中学到大学的过渡。

sentences.english: New students are going to have to be sociable as well – not just relying on old friends at home.
sentences.chinese: 新生还得学会社交——不能只依赖家乡的老朋友。

sentences.english: Going to university requires meeting new people and making new friends.
sentences.chinese: 上大学就意味着要结识陌生人，结交新朋友。

sentences.english: This often begins in Freshers’ Week although journalism student Emmeke Megannety warns that: “People starting uni need to remember that the people you meet in your first week will not necessarily be your friends for life.”
sentences.chinese: 这通常从新生周就开始了，不过新闻系学生埃梅克·梅加内蒂提醒道：“刚开始上大学的人要记住，你第一周遇到的人，未必会成为你一辈子的朋友。”

sentences.english: But whatever your expectations, it’s good to be prepared for the time of your life.
sentences.chinese: 但无论你对大学生活有着怎样的期待，做好充分准备，才能迎接这段人生中最美好的时光。

title: How to be more resilient
titleChinese: 什么是 AQ？聊聊如何提高你的适应力
paragraphs: We’ve all heard of IQ, and terms like EQ, which relates to your emotional intelligence, are commonly used. But have you heard of AQ? AQ stands for adversity quotient and measures your ability to deal with the ups and downs of life. Being able to handle these rough patches we all go through is not only important in our personal lives but in our professional lives too. So how can we learn to be more resilient?

Adverse situations can take us by surprise and shock us. In the workplace, it could be in the form of redundancies, the company we work for going under or being restructured, or even missing out on a promotion. Failed friendships and relationships, financial hard times and even bereavements are things that can occur outside of work. AQ measures our ability to withstand the shocks when life throws curveballs at us – how likely we are to crumble or thrive in these situations. It can be used to predict our attitudes, perseverance, longevity, and the way we learn from changes in environment. In short, our resilience when there is a drastic change.

Luckily, there are some steps you can take to help you be more resilient and adaptable in the face of adversity, according to Dr Shahram Heshmat, professor of health economics at the University of Illinois. First, try and find a meaningful goal. Resilient people often have an aim and are able to concentrate more on a desired outcome, seeing negative situations as a bump in the road on the way to achieving their goal. Learning to relax and regulate your emotions is another key step – one way to help you destress is by practising breathing exercises. Likewise, dwelling on things and letting them get to you can cause you to be stressed. See difficulties more as an opportunity to learn and grow emotionally. Finally, make sure you have a good social support network. Being able to talk with someone about the challenges we face can help.
Things happen in life we can’t prevent – and sometimes they aren’t pleasant. But, taking a few steps to be more resilient can make them a little easier to get through.

vocabulary.entry: adversity quotient /ədˈvɜːsəti ˈkwəʊʃnt/ n. 逆境商数（AQ）
vocabulary.example: Adversity quotient is a key predictor of success in challenging environments.
vocabulary.translation: 逆境商数是预测人在充满挑战的环境中能否成功的关键指标。

vocabulary.entry: rough patch /rʌf pætʃ/ n. 困境；难关
vocabulary.example: The company went through a rough patch during the economic recession.
vocabulary.translation: 这家公司在经济衰退期遭遇了一段难关。

vocabulary.entry: resilient /rɪˈzɪliənt/ adj. 有韧性的；适应力强的
vocabulary.example: She is a resilient person who never gives up in the face of failure.
vocabulary.translation: 她是个韧性很强的人，面对失败从不气馁。

vocabulary.entry: redundancy /rɪˈdʌndənsi/ n. 裁员；解雇
vocabulary.example: The factory announced 50 redundancies due to falling sales.
vocabulary.translation: 由于销量下滑，这家工厂宣布裁员50人。

vocabulary.entry: go under /ɡəʊ ˈʌndə/ v. 倒闭；破产
vocabulary.example: Many small businesses went under during the pandemic.
vocabulary.translation: 疫情期间，许多小企业都倒闭了。

vocabulary.entry: restructure /ˌriːˈstrʌktʃə/ v. 重组；调整结构
vocabulary.example: The board decided to restructure the company's management team.
vocabulary.translation: 董事会决定重组公司的管理团队。

vocabulary.entry: bereavement /bɪˈriːvmənt/ n. 丧亲之痛；丧失亲人
vocabulary.example: She took a month off work to cope with her bereavement.
vocabulary.translation: 她请了一个月假来平复丧亲之痛。

vocabulary.entry: withstand /wɪðˈstænd/ v. 承受；抵挡
vocabulary.example: The material can withstand high temperatures and harsh weather.
vocabulary.translation: 这种材料能承受高温和恶劣天气。

vocabulary.entry: throw a curveball /θrəʊ ə ˈkɜːvbɔːl/ v. 抛出难题；制造意外麻烦
vocabulary.example: The sudden change in policy threw a curveball at all investors.
vocabulary.translation: 政策的突然变动给所有投资者都出了个难题。

vocabulary.entry: crumble /ˈkrʌmbl/ v. 崩溃；瓦解
vocabulary.example: His confidence crumbled after he failed the exam twice.
vocabulary.translation: 两次考试失利后，他的自信心彻底崩溃了。

vocabulary.entry: perseverance /ˌpɜːsəˈvɪərəns/ n. 毅力；坚韧不拔
vocabulary.example: Success requires hard work and perseverance.
vocabulary.translation: 成功需要努力和毅力。

vocabulary.entry: longevity /lɒnˈdʒevəti/ n. 长寿；持久力
vocabulary.example: A balanced diet contributes to longevity.
vocabulary.translation: 均衡饮食有助于延年益寿。

vocabulary.entry: drastic /ˈdræstɪk/ adj. 剧烈的；急剧的
vocabulary.example: The government has taken drastic measures to reduce inflation.
vocabulary.translation: 政府采取了激进措施来降低通货膨胀。

vocabulary.entry: adaptable /əˈdæptəbl/ adj. 能适应的；适应性强的
vocabulary.example: Young people are usually more adaptable to new environments.
vocabulary.translation: 年轻人通常更能适应新环境。

vocabulary.entry: bump in the road /bʌmp ɪn ðə rəʊd/ n. 小挫折；小障碍
vocabulary.example: This delay is just a bump in the road; we will still meet the deadline.
vocabulary.translation: 这次延误只是个小插曲，我们还是能赶上截止日期的。

vocabulary.entry: regulate /ˈreɡjuleɪt/ v. 调节；控制
vocabulary.example: Hormones help to regulate various bodily functions.
vocabulary.translation: 荷尔蒙有助于调节人体的各项机能。

vocabulary.entry: destress /ˌdiːˈstres/ v. 缓解压力；减压
vocabulary.example: Yoga and meditation are great ways to destress after work.
vocabulary.translation: 瑜伽和冥想是下班后减压的好方法。

vocabulary.entry: breathing exercise /ˈbriːðɪŋ ˈeksəsaɪz/ n. 呼吸练习
vocabulary.example: Doing breathing exercises every morning can improve lung function.
vocabulary.translation: 每天早上做呼吸练习能改善肺功能。

vocabulary.entry: dwell on /dwel ɒn/ v. 纠结于；念念不忘
vocabulary.example: Don't dwell on past mistakes; focus on the future.
vocabulary.translation: 不要纠结于过去的错误，要着眼于未来。

vocabulary.entry: social support network /ˈsəʊʃl səˈpɔːt ˈnetwɜːk/ n. 社交支持网络
vocabulary.example: A strong social support network is crucial for mental health.
vocabulary.translation: 强大的社交支持网络对心理健康至关重要。

vocabulary.entry: predict /prɪˈdɪkt/ v. 预测；预言
vocabulary.example: The weather forecast predicts rain for tomorrow.
vocabulary.translation: 天气预报预测明天有雨。

vocabulary.entry: financial hard time /faɪˈnænʃl hɑːd taɪm/ n. 经济困难时期
vocabulary.example: Many families faced financial hard times during the energy crisis.
vocabulary.translation: 能源危机期间，许多家庭都陷入了经济困境。

vocabulary.entry: miss out on /mɪs aʊt ɒn/ v. 错失；错过
vocabulary.example: He missed out on the scholarship because of his poor grades.
vocabulary.translation: 他因为成绩差而错失了奖学金。

vocabulary.entry: promotion /prəˈməʊʃn/ n. 晋升；提拔
vocabulary.example: She got a promotion to manager after working hard for two years.
vocabulary.translation: 努力工作两年后，她被提拔为经理。

vocabulary.entry: thrive /θraɪv/ v. 茁壮成长；蓬勃发展
vocabulary.example: Plants thrive in warm, sunny conditions.
vocabulary.translation: 植物在温暖向阳的环境中长势良好。

sentences.chinese: 但你听说过逆商（AQ）吗？

sentences.english: AQ stands for adversity quotient and measures your ability to deal with the ups and downs of life.
sentences.chinese: 逆商的全称是逆境商数，它衡量的是一个人应对人生起伏的能力。

sentences.chinese: 能否妥善处理这些我们都会经历的困境，不仅在个人生活中至关重要，在职业生涯里亦是如此。

sentences.english: So how can we learn to be more resilient?
sentences.chinese: 那么，我们该如何学会让自己更具韧性呢？

sentences.english: Adverse situations can take us by surprise and shock us.
sentences.chinese: 逆境往往来得猝不及防，让我们措手不及。

sentences.english: In the workplace, it could be in the form of redundancies, the company we work for going under or being restructured, or even missing out on a promotion.
sentences.chinese: 职场中，逆境可能表现为被裁员、供职的公司倒闭或重组，甚至是错失晋升机会。

sentences.english: Failed friendships and relationships, financial hard times and even bereavements are things that can occur outside of work.
sentences.chinese: 而职场之外，也可能遭遇友情破裂、感情失败、经济拮据乃至痛失亲友等变故。

sentences.english: AQ measures our ability to withstand the shocks when life throws curveballs at us – how likely we are to crumble or thrive in these situations.
sentences.chinese: 逆商衡量的是，当生活向我们抛出难题时，我们承受冲击的能力——在这些处境下，我们是丢盔弃甲还是迎难而上。

sentences.english: It can be used to predict our attitudes, perseverance, longevity, and the way we learn from changes in environment.
sentences.chinese: 它可以用来预测我们的态度、毅力、耐力，以及我们从环境变化中学习的方式。

sentences.english: In short, our resilience when there is a drastic change.
sentences.chinese: 简而言之，逆商体现的是我们面对剧变时的韧性。

sentences.english: Luckily, there are some steps you can take to help you be more resilient and adaptable in the face of adversity, according to Dr Shahram Heshmat, professor of health economics at the University of Illinois.
sentences.chinese: 伊利诺伊大学健康经济学教授沙赫拉姆·赫什马特博士表示，幸运的是，我们可以通过一些方法，让自己在逆境面前更具韧性和适应能力。

sentences.english: First, try and find a meaningful goal.
sentences.chinese: 首先，树立一个有意义的目标。

sentences.english: Resilient people often have an aim and are able to concentrate more on a desired outcome, seeing negative situations as a bump in the road on the way to achieving their goal.
sentences.chinese: 韧性强的人通常都有明确的目标，能够更专注于想要的结果，将困境视为实现目标路上的小坎坷。

sentences.english: Learning to relax and regulate your emotions is another key step – one way to help you destress is by practising breathing exercises.
sentences.chinese: 其次，学会放松和调节情绪，呼吸练习就是一种缓解压力的有效方式。

sentences.english: Likewise, dwelling on things and letting them get to you can cause you to be stressed.
sentences.chinese: 同样，一味纠结于烦心事、让负面情绪影响自己，会导致压力倍增。

sentences.english: See difficulties more as an opportunity to learn and grow emotionally.
sentences.chinese: 不妨把困难看作是学习和心智成长的机会。

sentences.english: Finally, make sure you have a good social support network.
sentences.chinese: 最后，建立良好的社交支持网络。

sentences.english: Being able to talk with someone about the challenges we face can help.
sentences.chinese: 能向他人倾诉自己面临的挑战，本身就是一种帮助。

sentences.english: Things happen in life we can’t prevent – and sometimes they aren’t pleasant.
sentences.chinese: 生活中总会发生一些我们无法预料的事——有时这些事并不令人愉快。

sentences.english: But, taking a few steps to be more resilient can make them a little easier to get through.
sentences.chinese: 但只要采取一些方法提升韧性，我们就能更从容地度过这些难关。

title: Do we still need to write by hand
titleChinese: 数码时代用手写字有什么好处？
paragraphs: When did you last write a letter? Properly write one – by hand? In a digital world, where sending a text or email is far more convenient than using snail mail, is the writing on the wall for traditional pen and paper? Well, some people claim that writing still has many benefits, so maybe it’s not time to ditch your ballpoint or fountain pen yet.

These days, when people request things in writing, a typed, electronic document will be accepted. Doing this on a computer means it could be saved, edited, duplicated and sent via email. But crafting a handwritten document is unique: It requires planning and thought, and, as well as practising your handwriting, it helps you to remember spelling and punctuation.

Some experts believe your brain benefits from using old-fashioned pen and paper. This is particularly relevant for students, where typing notes into a laptop is thought to lack the ‘tactile feedback’ to the brain that contact between pen and paper does. BBC Worklife website quotes Hetty Roessingh from the University of Calgary, who says that “taking notes by hand involves cognitive engagement in summarising, paraphrasing, organising, concept and vocabulary mapping.” Others agree that handwriting may boost fine motor skills in your hands and fingers.

There are everyday benefits to using pen and paper too. Scribbling notes, shopping lists or messages on the back of an envelope can still be useful, quick and portable. But putting pen to paper in a letter to a friend or loved one can probably have the most impact. Pen pal writer Katherine Moller told the BBC: “In a world where it is so easy to hop online to email or to send a fast text, it is so personal and so precious to know someone chose to turn off the virtual world to spend some time with you.”
So, while digital skills remain important, don’t write off your pens and pencils yet – especially if your smartphone, tablet or laptop runs out of power!

vocabulary.entry: snail mail /ˈsneɪl meɪl/ n. 平信（邮寄速度慢的传统信件）
vocabulary.example: I prefer sending snail mail to my grandparents as they don't use emails often.
vocabulary.translation: 我更喜欢给祖父母寄平信，因为他们不常使用电子邮件。

vocabulary.entry: writing on the wall /ˈraɪtɪŋ ɒn ðə wɔːl/ n. 不祥之兆；败亡的预兆
vocabulary.example: The declining sales figures are the writing on the wall for the small bookstore.
vocabulary.translation: 不断下滑的销售额对这家小书店来说是个不祥之兆。

vocabulary.entry: ditch /dɪtʃ/ v. 丢弃；抛弃
vocabulary.example: She decided to ditch her old textbooks after graduating from college.
vocabulary.translation: 大学毕业后，她决定把旧课本都扔掉。

vocabulary.entry: ballpoint /ˈbɔːlpɔɪnt/ n. 圆珠笔
vocabulary.example: He always keeps a ballpoint in his pocket for taking quick notes.
vocabulary.translation: 他口袋里总装着一支圆珠笔，方便随手记笔记。

vocabulary.entry: fountain pen /ˈfaʊntən pen/ n. 钢笔
vocabulary.example: My father gave me a vintage fountain pen as my 18th birthday gift.
vocabulary.translation: 父亲送了我一支复古钢笔作为我的18岁生日礼物。

vocabulary.entry: duplicate /ˈdjuːplɪkeɪt/ v. 复制；复印
vocabulary.example: The secretary was asked to duplicate the report for all attendees.
vocabulary.translation: 秘书被要求为所有参会者复印这份报告。

vocabulary.entry: craft /krɑːft/ v. 精心制作；构思
vocabulary.example: She spent hours crafting a heartfelt speech for her friend's wedding.
vocabulary.translation: 她花了好几个小时，为朋友的婚礼精心撰写了一篇真挚的演讲稿。

vocabulary.entry: punctuation /ˌpʌŋktʃuˈeɪʃn/ n. 标点符号
vocabulary.example: Proper punctuation is essential for clear and effective writing.
vocabulary.translation: 正确使用标点符号对于清晰高效的写作至关重要。

vocabulary.entry: tactile feedback /ˈtæktaɪl ˈfiːdbæk/ n. 触觉反馈
vocabulary.example: Touchscreen devices provide tactile feedback to simulate button presses.
vocabulary.translation: 触屏设备会提供触觉反馈，来模拟按键的触感。

vocabulary.entry: cognitive engagement /ˈkɒɡnətɪv ɪnˈɡeɪdʒmənt/ n. 认知参与
vocabulary.example: The puzzle game requires high cognitive engagement from players.
vocabulary.translation: 这款益智游戏需要玩家高度投入认知能力。

vocabulary.entry: summarise /ˈsʌməraɪz/ v. 总结；概述
vocabulary.example: The teacher asked students to summarise the main idea of the passage.
vocabulary.translation: 老师要求学生们总结这篇文章的主旨。

vocabulary.entry: paraphrase /ˈpærəfreɪz/ v. 释义；意译
vocabulary.example: You should paraphrase the quote instead of copying it directly in your essay.
vocabulary.translation: 你应该把这段引文意译出来，而不是直接抄到论文里。

vocabulary.entry: vocabulary mapping /vəˈkæbjələri ˈmæpɪŋ/ n. 词汇脉络构建
vocabulary.example: Vocabulary mapping helps students connect new words with existing knowledge.
vocabulary.translation: 词汇脉络构建能帮助学生将生词与已有知识联系起来。

vocabulary.entry: fine motor skill /faɪn ˈməʊtə skɪl/ n. 精细运动能力
vocabulary.example: Drawing and painting can improve children's fine motor skills.
vocabulary.translation: 绘画能提升儿童的精细运动能力。

vocabulary.entry: scribble /ˈskrɪbl/ v. 潦草地写；随手记下
vocabulary.example: He scribbled a phone number on a piece of paper and lost it soon after.
vocabulary.translation: 他在一张纸上潦草地记下了一个电话号码，没过多久就弄丢了。

vocabulary.entry: portable /ˈpɔːtəbl/ adj. 便携的；手提式的
vocabulary.example: This portable notebook is perfect for taking notes while travelling.
vocabulary.translation: 这款便携笔记本非常适合旅行时记笔记。

vocabulary.entry: pen pal /ˈpen pæl/ n. 笔友
vocabulary.example: She has a pen pal in France who she writes to once a month.
vocabulary.translation: 她有一个法国笔友，每月都会给对方写一封信。

vocabulary.entry: virtual world /ˈvɜːtʃuəl wɜːld/ n. 虚拟世界
vocabulary.example: Many teenagers spend a lot of time in the virtual world of online games.
vocabulary.translation: 许多青少年会花大量时间沉浸在网络游戏的虚拟世界里。

vocabulary.entry: write off /raɪt ɒf/ v. 摒弃；不再考虑
vocabulary.example: Don't write off his suggestion without giving it a second thought.
vocabulary.translation: 别不假思索就否定他的建议。

vocabulary.entry: tablet /ˈtæblət/ n. 平板电脑
vocabulary.example: She uses a tablet to read e-books and watch online courses.
vocabulary.translation: 她用平板电脑阅读电子书和观看在线课程。

vocabulary.entry: run out of power /rʌn aʊt ɒv ˈpaʊə/ 没电；耗尽电量
vocabulary.example: My phone ran out of power halfway through the concert.
vocabulary.translation: 音乐会进行到一半时，我的手机就没电了。

vocabulary.entry: vintage /ˈvɪntɪdʒ/ adj. 复古的；老式的
vocabulary.example: She likes to collect vintage postcards from different countries.
vocabulary.translation: 她喜欢收集来自不同国家的复古明信片。

vocabulary.entry: heartfelt /ˈhɑːtfelt/ adj. 真挚的；由衷的
vocabulary.example: He gave a heartfelt apology for his mistake at the meeting.
vocabulary.translation: 他在会议上为自己的失误诚恳地道歉。

vocabulary.entry: relevant /ˈreləvənt/ adj. 相关的；切题的
vocabulary.example: Please provide relevant documents to support your application.
vocabulary.translation: 请提供相关文件来支持你的申请。

vocabulary.entry: essential /ɪˈsenʃl/ adj. 极其重要的；必不可少的
vocabulary.example: Water and food are essential for human survival.
vocabulary.translation: 水和食物是人类生存必不可少的东西。

sentences.english: When did you last write a letter?
sentences.chinese: 你上一次写信是什么时候？

sentences.english: Properly write one – by hand?
sentences.chinese: 规规矩矩的用手写的那种信？

sentences.english: In a digital world, where sending a text or email is far more convenient than using snail mail, is the writing on the wall for traditional pen and paper?
sentences.chinese: 在这个数字时代，发信息或邮件远比寄平信方便得多，传统的纸笔书写是否已经穷途末路了呢？

sentences.english: Well, some people claim that writing still has many benefits, so maybe it’s not time to ditch your ballpoint or fountain pen yet.
sentences.chinese: 其实，有些人认为手写依然益处良多，所以或许现在还不是扔掉圆珠笔或钢笔的时候。

sentences.english: These days, when people request things in writing, a typed, electronic document will be accepted.
sentences.chinese: 如今，当人们要求提供书面材料时，打印的电子文档也是可以被接受的。

sentences.english: Doing this on a computer means it could be saved, edited, duplicated and sent via email.
sentences.chinese: 用电脑制作文档，意味着内容可以被保存、编辑、复制，还能通过邮件发送。

sentences.english: But crafting a handwritten document is unique: It requires planning and thought, and, as well as practising your handwriting, it helps you to remember spelling and punctuation.
sentences.chinese: 但手写文档的创作过程是独一无二的：它需要事先构思和思考，而且在练习书写的同时，还能帮助你牢记拼写和标点的用法。

sentences.english: This is particularly relevant for students, where typing notes into a laptop is thought to lack the ‘tactile feedback’ to the brain that contact between pen and paper does.

title: Could lending affect your friendship
titleChinese: 借钱会影响你的友谊吗？
paragraphs: Shakespeare once wrote: ‘Neither a borrower nor a lender be; For loan oft loses both itself and friend’. It’s often paraphrased and used as a warning about the dangers of lending, and how you could risk a friendship through it. But why can lending money be so detrimental to our friendships?

If our friend or family member comes to us for hard cash, it can be very difficult to turn them away. You feel under pressure to help. And if that money doesn’t come back, it can lead to fights or even legal battles. So how can we, as the lender, avoid these complications? According to Bradley T. Klontz, an expert in financial psychology, there are some steps you can take.

Understanding why there is an inevitable risk to lending anything to a friend is the first thing. And it’s not just the risk of losing the money, but the friendship could also be in danger. This is because, psychologically speaking, the action of lending has changed the balance of power. The lender becomes superior, while the borrower may feel awkward with the new arrangement. Likewise, if you try to advise them on what to do with the money, it might make things difficult between you two. In other words, let go – and see it as their money.

And if you can’t afford to lend something, don’t. Saying ‘no’ is hard when a friend comes asking, but if you need that money, denying them is probably the safest course of action. If you still feel the need to lend, making a legally binding agreement and putting things down in writing could guarantee instalments or deadlines. But, some friends may not take too kindly to being asked to make it official – seeing it as a lack of trust.

Finally, for some, it’s best to just see the money as a gift and be pleasantly surprised if something comes back. And if you do want to preserve your friendship, when you need to borrow some money, perhaps a bank is a better option.

title: Why we forget
paragraphs: How is your memory? Remembering things is an important function of our brain – if we can’t recall how to do something, we can’t survive. If you think about it, there is so much we have to remember – from where we left our car keys to how we walk. Maybe it’s no surprise that sometimes we are forgetful.

Memory allows the brain to store and retrieve information when required. Our short-term memory can hold a small amount of information for a short time, while our long-term memory can hold an unlimited amount of information for a long time. Our memory is amazing, but why do we still forget things?

It’s possible we don’t always store information in our memory effectively, maybe because we are in a rush or we consider it irrelevant at the time. When we do store information, we often make connections with other things, which helps us recall it later. If you don’t have these connections, then it can be easier to forget. Writing for the BBC’s Science Focus magazine, Luis Villazon says “It is also possible that memories decay over time. As they have not been revisited, their biological ‘trace’ becomes weak.” It’s true that if you don’t perform a task for a long period of time, it can be difficult to recall how to do it. This could be because, just like in a computer, our memory is full, or that our short-term memory is easier to access.

But sometimes even our short-term memory can let us down. Have you ever gone into a room to fetch something only to forget what you wanted when you got there? This is called ‘The Doorway Effect’. Writing for the BBC Future website, psychologist Tom Stafford explains that this “occurs because we change both the physical and mental environments, moving to a different room and thinking about different things.” Put simply, we are metaphorically trying to spin too many plates at the same time.

So, if you have a mind like a sieve, it could be because you have too much on your mind. But we do need to keep our memory sharp by continually using it, especially as beyond our 50s our brains tend to shrink in volume and our memory begins to decline. That’s when we’re at more risk of getting Alzheimer’s disease.
However, as Luis Villazon says, “Forgetting is not always a bad thing! It would waste cognitive resources if we remembered every detail of the world around us.” That’s something worth remembering!

sentences.english: It’s possible we don’t always store information in our memory effectively, maybe because we are in a rush or we consider it irrelevant at the time.
sentences.chinese: 我们未能有效储存信息，可能是因为当时很匆忙，或是觉得这些信息无关紧要。

sentences.english: When we do store information, we often make connections with other things, which helps us recall it later.
sentences.chinese: 当我们储存信息时，往往会将其与其他事物建立关联，这有助于我们日后回忆。

sentences.english: If you don’t have these connections, then it can be easier to forget.
sentences.chinese: 如果没有这些关联，信息就更容易被遗忘。

sentences.english: Writing for the BBC’s Science Focus magazine, Luis Villazon says “It is also possible that memories decay over time.
sentences.chinese: 路易斯·维拉松在为英国广播公司《科学焦点》杂志撰稿时表示：“记忆也可能会随着时间的推移而淡化。

sentences.english: As they have not been revisited, their biological ‘trace’ becomes weak.”
sentences.chinese: 由于长期没有被唤醒，它们的生物‘痕迹’会逐渐变弱。”

sentences.english: It’s true that if you don’t perform a task for a long period of time, it can be difficult to recall how to do it.
sentences.chinese: 确实，一项技能如果长期不使用，我们就可能会忘记操作方法。

sentences.english: This could be because, just like in a computer, our memory is full, or that our short-term memory is easier to access.
sentences.chinese: 这或许是因为和电脑一样，我们的记忆存储空间已满，也可能是因为短时记忆的调取更为便捷。

sentences.english: But sometimes even our short-term memory can let us down.
sentences.chinese: 但有时候，就连我们的短时记忆也会靠不住。

sentences.english: Have you ever gone into a room to fetch something only to forget what you wanted when you got there?
sentences.chinese: 你有没有过这样的经历：走进房间想拿某样东西，可一进门就忘了要拿什么？

sentences.english: This is called ‘The Doorway Effect’.
sentences.chinese: 这种现象被称为“门口效应”。

sentences.english: Writing for the BBC Future website, psychologist Tom Stafford explains that this “occurs because we change both the physical and mental environments, moving to a different room and thinking about different things.”
sentences.chinese: 心理学家汤姆·斯塔福德在为英国广播公司未来网撰稿时解释道，这种现象的发生是因为“我们的物理环境和心理状态都发生了变化——走进了另一个房间，脑子里想的事情也不一样了。”

sentences.english: Put simply, we are metaphorically trying to spin too many plates at the same time.
sentences.chinese: 简单来说，这就好比我们同时要兼顾太多事情，顾此失彼。

sentences.english: So, if you have a mind like a sieve, it could be because you have too much on your mind.
sentences.chinese: 因此，如果你的脑子像个筛子，总是丢三落四，可能是因为脑子里的事情太多了。

sentences.english: But we do need to keep our memory sharp by continually using it, especially as beyond our 50s our brains tend to shrink in volume and our memory begins to decline. That’s when we’re at more risk of getting Alzheimer’s disease.
sentences.chinese: 但我们确实需要通过不断使用来保持记忆力的敏锐，尤其是在50岁以后，大脑体积会逐渐萎缩，记忆力也会开始衰退，此时我们患上阿尔茨海默病的风险也会更高。

sentences.english: However, as Luis Villazon says, “Forgetting is not always a bad thing!
sentences.chinese: 不过，正如路易斯·维拉松所说：“遗忘并非总是坏事！

sentences.english: It would waste cognitive resources if we remembered every detail of the world around us.”
sentences.chinese: 如果我们记住周围世界的每一个细节，那会浪费大量的认知资源。”

sentences.english: That’s something worth remembering!
sentences.chinese: 这一点，倒是值得我们铭记于心。

title: The cost of going to a wedding
paragraphs: Weddings are expensive affairs – there’s nothing new or surprising in that statement. When we talk about the costs of a wedding, we often think about the financial toll on the person paying for it. The outlay on tiered cakes, the dress with a long train, appliques and veil, and canapes at the reception can all add up. But what about the guests? The cost to your friends and family to attend.

The first thing to think about when attending is the price of getting there. Even just a few hundred miles from where you live can bring some expenses – be it transport or staying in a hotel. But some people like to tie the knot in exotic locations, thinking it will make their special day even more special – on a beach in front of palm trees rather than somewhere closer to home. Going to far-flung corners of the Earth to watch the event can really be a dealbreaker for some when deciding if they can make it.

Then there is the gift. What do you give a person on their wedding day? In some cultures, asking for money isn’t the done thing. Sometimes the bride and groom may issue a list of items they want to receive that you have to pick from. But what do you buy? And if it’s money, how much do you give them? How much is too much? These are questions all attendees face – give too little and you may cause offence, too much and you may be out of pocket. And of course, you don’t want to be outdone by a friend giving more than you.

Finally, the last thing you want to feel when going to a wedding is regret about the amount you’ve spent. If you give a good gift and spend a lot on getting there, and the event isn’t great, or the food at the reception isn’t perfect, you might feel a little resentment. Therefore, only give what you can afford to give. Weddings can be expensive for everyone concerned. But people often overlook the cost for guests. In the end, though, that special day is supposed to be a celebration of love above anything else.

sentences.english: Going to far-flung corners of the Earth to watch the event can really be a dealbreaker for some when deciding if they can make it.

sentences.english: Then there is the gift.

sentences.chinese: 婚礼当天，该给新人送点什么呢？

title: The benefits of learning a musical instrument
paragraphs: It’s difficult not to admire the talent of a skilled musician. Whether it be a pianist, flautist or cellist, these individuals have shown dedication and passion over a long period of time to reach the highest levels of performance. But they say it’s never too late to learn. So what are the benefits, for both children and adults, in learning a musical instrument?

Learning to play a musical instrument when growing up can improve hearing in adulthood. According to a study by Dr Nina Kraus, Professor of Neurobiology at Northwestern University in Illinois, US, children who played musical instruments were better at recognising different frequencies. This improved hearing skill carried over into later life with adults who had once played an instrument able to discern sounds of different pitches more easily. And it could also have some academic benefits too. A study conducted by the University of British Columbia found that students who engaged in music-related activities during grades 7-12 scored significantly higher in science, English and maths.

And there are not just benefits to children. Whether you choose to play the piano, pick or strum a guitar or learn a drumbeat, you could end up joining a band or orchestra. This in turn could improve your social life, meeting other bandmates who are likeminded in their love of a good tune. Learning an instrument can also give you a sense of achievement. Nailing that perfect chord is one way, but what if you got together with a bunch of friends and entered into a battle of the bands – and won?
So, whether you’re looking to destress playing out some chords, or improve your grades at school, maybe taking up an instrument could help you.

vocabulary.entry: frequency /ˈfriːkwənsi/ n. 频率；音频

vocabulary.entry: academic /ˌækəˈdemɪk/ adj. 学业的；学术的

vocabulary.translation: 这所学校提供多种学术活动来丰富学生的知识储备。

vocabulary.entry: strum /strʌm/ v. （漫不经心地）弹拨；扫弦

vocabulary.translation: 他喜欢一边弹拨吉他，一边唱民谣。

vocabulary.entry: drumbeat /ˈdrʌmbiːt/ n. 鼓点；鼓的节奏
vocabulary.example: The steady drumbeat set the pace for the whole song.
vocabulary.translation: 平稳的鼓点为整首歌奠定了节奏。

vocabulary.entry: orchestra /ˈɔːkɪstrə/ n. 管弦乐团

vocabulary.translation: 市管弦乐团本周末将演奏贝多芬的交响曲。

vocabulary.entry: likeminded /ˈlaɪkmaɪndɪd/ adj. 志同道合的

vocabulary.translation: 她在音乐研习班上结识了一群志同道合的人。

vocabulary.entry: tune /tjuːn/ n. 曲调；旋律
vocabulary.example: This old tune always reminds me of my childhood.
vocabulary.translation: 这首老歌的旋律总能让我想起童年时光。

vocabulary.entry: achievement /əˈtʃiːvmənt/ n. 成就；成绩
vocabulary.example: Winning the competition is a great achievement for the young musician.
vocabulary.translation: 赢得比赛对这位年轻的音乐家来说是一项巨大的成就。

vocabulary.entry: chord /kɔːd/ n. 和弦

vocabulary.translation: 他们的乐队在当地的乐队大赛中获得了一等奖。

vocabulary.entry: destress /ˌdiːˈstres/ v. 减压；缓解压力
vocabulary.example: Many people destress by listening to or playing music after work.
vocabulary.translation: 很多人下班后通过听音乐或演奏乐器来减压。

vocabulary.entry: take up /teɪk ʌp/ 开始学习；从事
vocabulary.example: She decided to take up the violin after watching a live performance.
vocabulary.translation: 看完一场现场演奏会后，她决定开始学习小提琴。

vocabulary.entry: passion /ˈpæʃn/ n. 热爱；酷爱
vocabulary.example: Her passion for music has never faded over the years.
vocabulary.translation: 这些年来，她对音乐的热爱从未消退。

vocabulary.entry: performance /pəˈfɔːməns/ n. 演奏；表演
vocabulary.example: The pianist's performance received a standing ovation from the audience.
vocabulary.translation: 这位钢琴家的演奏赢得了观众的起立鼓掌。

vocabulary.entry: benefit /ˈbenɪfɪt/ n. 益处；好处
vocabulary.example: Regular exercise has many benefits for physical and mental health.
vocabulary.translation: 规律运动对身心健康有诸多益处。

vocabulary.entry: engage /ɪnˈɡeɪdʒ/ v. 参与；参加
vocabulary.example: Students are encouraged to engage in extracurricular activities at school.

sentences.english: It’s difficult not to admire the talent of a skilled musician.

sentences.english: Learning to play a musical instrument when growing up can improve hearing in adulthood.
sentences.chinese: 年少时学习演奏乐器，有助于提升成年后的听力水平。

sentences.english: According to a study by Dr Nina Kraus, Professor of Neurobiology at Northwestern University in Illinois, US, children who played musical instruments were better at recognising different frequencies.
sentences.chinese: 美国伊利诺伊州西北大学神经生物学教授妮娜·克劳斯博士的一项研究表明，学过乐器的儿童更善于分辨不同的音频。

sentences.english: This improved hearing skill carried over into later life with adults who had once played an instrument able to discern sounds of different pitches more easily.
sentences.chinese: 这种提升后的听力技能会延续到日后的生活中，曾学过乐器的成年人能更轻松地辨别不同音高的声音。

sentences.english: A study conducted by the University of British Columbia found that students who engaged in music-related activities during grades 7-12 scored significantly higher in science, English and maths.
sentences.chinese: 英属哥伦比亚大学的一项研究发现，在7至12年级期间参与过音乐相关活动的学生，在科学、英语和数学学科的成绩要显著更高。

sentences.chinese: 学习乐器的益处并非只针对儿童。

sentences.english: Whether you choose to play the piano, pick or strum a guitar or learn a drumbeat, you could end up joining a band or orchestra.
sentences.chinese: 无论你选择弹钢琴、拨弄吉他、扫弦，还是学习打鼓，最终都有可能加入一支乐队或管弦乐团。

sentences.english: This in turn could improve your social life, meeting other bandmates who are likeminded in their love of a good tune.
sentences.chinese: 这进而能丰富你的社交生活，结识其他志同道合、同样热爱美妙旋律的乐队伙伴。

sentences.english: Nailing that perfect chord is one way, but what if you got together with a bunch of friends and entered into a battle of the bands – and won?
sentences.chinese: 弹出一组完美的和弦是一种成就，但如果你和一群朋友组队参加乐队大赛并夺冠，那种成就感又会是怎样的呢？

title: What’s the best way to read a book
paragraphs: Do you like to bury your head in a good book? Getting absorbed in a good story is a great way to relax. It improves your literacy, and, according to some experts, it’s good for your health as well. Studies show that it can increase our emotional intelligence as we understand a range of perspectives and motivations. But despite these benefits, does the way we consume a story make any difference?

For the purist, the only way to digest a good story is with a paperback or hardback book. Being in print, it’s possible to feel and even smell the book. And of course it’s very portable. But the traditional book has had a rival in recent years from e-books, which are read on e-readers or tablets. An ‘electronic’ book enables you to store hundreds of virtual books in one place and allows you to download books directly.

The e-book has become popular in schools, too, and according to one school in London, it’s encouraged more children to read. 11-year-old Summit told the BBC: “If you really want a book, you can just get it online. It’s so easy, and it’s made me read more. I probably read every day now.” For adults, e-books are certainly a lightweight way of accessing our favourite literature on the move.

The recent lockdowns due to the coronavirus pandemic have certainly given us all time to read more, and in the UK at least, sales of physical books have risen strongly. Last year, some 202 million paperbacks and hardbacks were sold, and the publishing industry hopes this trend will continue now that people have got into the habit of reading more.

But for those who can’t or don’t want to look at the text in a book, there are audiobooks to listen to. According to Clare Thorpe, writing for the BBC Culture website: “There are hugely ambitious productions using ensemble casts, specially created soundscapes and technological advances… some authors are even skipping print and writing exclusive audio content.” No matter what your reading preference, there’s no doubt we are spoilt for choice in how we access a good story.

title: Achieving net zero
titleChinese: 气候变化挑战下如何实现“净零排放”
paragraphs: We are all aware of the effect greenhouse gas emissions is having on our planet and the efforts needed to tackle climate change. Most of us are doing our bit to minimise our impact on the environment, but despite our collective effort, are we doing enough to achieve net zero by 2050?

Net zero means not adding to the amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. Many countries are doing their bit by changing how they generate and use power, thereby cutting carbon dioxide output. And they announced what further steps they were going to take at the recent COP26 summit in Glasgow.

In the UK, the government has been setting out its plans to achieve net zero by 2050. It’s recently announced an end date for the sale of gas boilers, which are used for heating homes. The idea is to replace them with heat pumps. It’s offering homeowners grants of up to £5,000 to get them installed. Another initiative in the UK is a big push towards electric vehicles. There are to be financial incentives for car manufacturers, and more charging points are to be installed in streets. And there’s to be a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2030.

But not all emissions can be reduced to zero, so those remaining will have to be compensated for, or offset. One way to do this is to plant thousands of trees, which are good at absorbing carbon dioxide. The UK government has pledged to plant 30,000 hectares of trees a year by 2025. There are other ideas too, but what’s certain is this will cost money. The CBI’s Tom Thackray told the BBC that “those costs have to be weighed up against the cost of inaction.”

Whether the UK, or anyone else, reaches net zero remains to be seen. And there’s some doubt about how this can be accurately measured anyway. But it’s generally recognised that a global effort is needed to tackle climate change. Therefore, net zero targets only make sense if every other country is moving in the same direction.

vocabulary.entry: greenhouse gas emission /ˈɡriːnhaʊs ɡæs iˈmɪʃn/ n. 温室气体排放

vocabulary.translation: 温室气体排放与全球气温上升密切相关。

vocabulary.entry: net zero /net ˈzɪərəʊ/ n. 净零排放

vocabulary.translation: 净零排放是许多国家环境政策的核心目标。

vocabulary.entry: climate change /ˈklaɪmət tʃeɪndʒ/ n. 气候变化
vocabulary.example: Climate change has led to more frequent extreme weather events.
vocabulary.translation: 气候变化导致极端天气事件愈发频繁。

vocabulary.entry: carbon dioxide /ˈkɑːbən daɪˈɒksaɪd/ n. 二氧化碳
vocabulary.example: Carbon dioxide is one of the main greenhouse gases.
vocabulary.translation: 二氧化碳是主要的温室气体之一。

vocabulary.entry: COP26 summit /ˌsiː əʊ ˈpiː ˈtwenti sɪks ˈsʌmɪt/ n. 第26届联合国气候变化大会
vocabulary.example: The COP26 summit focused on global cooperation to cut emissions.
vocabulary.translation: 第26届联合国气候变化大会聚焦于全球减排合作。

vocabulary.entry: gas boiler /ɡæs ˈbɔɪlə(r)/ n. 燃气锅炉
vocabulary.example: The old gas boiler in my house is inefficient and polluting.
vocabulary.translation: 我家那台旧燃气锅炉效率低且污染环境。

vocabulary.entry: heat pump /hiːt pʌmp/ n. 热泵

vocabulary.translation: 热泵可以从空气中提取热量为房屋供暖。

vocabulary.entry: grant /ɡrɑːnt/ n. 补贴；补助金
vocabulary.example: The government provides a grant for energy-efficient home improvements.
vocabulary.translation: 政府为高效节能的家居改造项目提供补贴。

vocabulary.translation: 这项新举措旨在推广可再生能源的使用。

vocabulary.entry: electric vehicle /ɪˈlektrɪk ˈviːəkl/ n. 电动汽车
vocabulary.example: More and more people are choosing to buy an electric vehicle.
vocabulary.translation: 越来越多的人选择购买电动汽车。
